nodes.name: Weil conjectures (Deligne's theorem)
nodes.statement: For a smooth projective variety over a finite field with q elements, the zeta function built from its numbers of points over the fields with q, q², q³, … elements is a rational function with a functional equation; the degrees of its factors are the variety's Betti numbers; and every Frobenius eigenvalue on cohomology of degree i has absolute value q^(i/2). The last part is the analogue of the Riemann Hypothesis.
nodes.by: Proposed by André Weil, 1949; rationality by Bernard Dwork, 1960; functional equation by Alexander Grothendieck, 1965; Riemann Hypothesis part by Pierre Deligne, 1974
nodes.note: Grothendieck hoped to prove the Riemann Hypothesis part from his standard conjectures. Deligne found a way around them, and the standard conjectures are still open.

nodes.name: Hasse–Weil bound (Riemann Hypothesis for curves over finite fields)
nodes.statement: A smooth projective curve of genus g over a finite field with q elements has N points, where |N − (q + 1)| ≤ 2g√q.
nodes.by: Helmut Hasse for elliptic curves (g = 1), 1933; André Weil for all curves, announced 1940, full proof published 1948
nodes.note: This is the curve case of the Weil conjectures. Weil's work on it led him to state the conjectures for all dimensions.

nodes.name: Weil bound for Kloosterman sums
nodes.statement: For a prime p and integers a, b not divisible by p, the Kloosterman sum K(a, b; p), the sum of e^(2πi(ax + bx⁻¹)/p) over x = 1, …, p − 1, has absolute value at most 2√p.
nodes.by: André Weil, 1948
nodes.note: Weil wrote the sum as a sum over the hyperbola xy = ab over the field with p elements and got the bound from the Riemann Hypothesis for an Artin–Schreier covering of that curve, whose zeta function has the Kloosterman sums in its factors.

nodes.name: Ramanujan's conjecture for the tau function (Deligne's theorem)
nodes.statement: The coefficients τ(n) of the modular form Δ = q ∏ (1 − qⁿ)²⁴ satisfy |τ(p)| ≤ 2p^(11/2) for every prime p.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Srinivasa Ramanujan, 1916; proven by Pierre Deligne, 1974
nodes.note: Deligne showed in 1969 (Bourbaki seminar, published 1971), using the Eichler–Shimura isomorphism and work of Kuga, Sato, Shimura and Ihara, that the bound follows from the Weil conjectures. His 1974 proof of their Riemann Hypothesis part finished it, and the same argument covers holomorphic cusp forms of weight 2 and more (Petersson's conjecture).

nodes.name: Batyrev's theorem on birational Calabi–Yau manifolds
nodes.statement: If two smooth complex projective varieties with trivial canonical bundle (Calabi–Yau manifolds) are birationally equivalent, they have the same Betti numbers.
nodes.by: Victor Batyrev, 1997 (published 1999)
nodes.note: Batyrev used p-adic integration to show that the two varieties have the same number of points over finite fields, then used Deligne's proof of the Weil conjectures to turn equal point counts into equal Betti numbers.

nodes.name: Katz–Messing theorem (Künneth standard conjecture over finite fields)
nodes.statement: For a smooth projective variety over a finite field, the projections of its cohomology onto each single degree are given by algebraic cycles. This is Grothendieck's standard conjecture C for such varieties.
nodes.by: Nicholas Katz and William Messing, 1974
nodes.note: Katz and Messing derived it from Deligne's Riemann Hypothesis for varieties over finite fields. Over the complex numbers the same conjecture is open in general.

nodes.name: Langlands functoriality conjecture
nodes.statement: A suitable map between the L-groups of two reductive groups should carry automorphic forms on one group to automorphic forms on the other, in a way that matches their L-functions. Applied to the trivial group, it predicts that complex representations of the Galois group correspond to automorphic forms, the part of Langlands reciprocity that covers Artin L-functions.
nodes.by: Robert Langlands, letter to André Weil 1967 and paper 1970
nodes.note: Harris and Taylor (2001) and Henniart (2000) proved the local correspondence for GL(n). Global functoriality over number fields is open in general. Known cases include symmetric-power lifts of holomorphic modular forms (Newton and Thorne, 2021).

nodes.name: Generalized Ramanujan conjecture
nodes.statement: Every cuspidal automorphic representation of GL(n) over a number field (more generally, every globally generic cuspidal representation of a reductive group) is tempered at every place. For holomorphic modular forms this is the Ramanujan–Petersson bound.
nodes.by: Ichirō Satake, 1966, recasting Ramanujan and Petersson's conjecture for automorphic representations
nodes.note: Functoriality for all symmetric powers of GL(n) would prove it. The holomorphic case is Deligne's theorem; the case of Maass forms is open because Deligne's method does not apply there.

nodes.name: Selberg's eigenvalue conjecture (1/4 conjecture)
nodes.statement: For every congruence subgroup of SL(2, ℤ), the eigenvalues of the Laplace operator on its Maass cusp forms are all at least 1/4.
nodes.by: Atle Selberg, 1965
nodes.note: It is the generalized Ramanujan conjecture for GL(2) over the rationals at the infinite place. Selberg proved the bound 3/16; the best known bound, 975/4096 ≈ 0.238, is due to Kim and Sarnak (2003).

nodes.name: Artin holomorphy conjecture
nodes.statement: For a Galois extension of number fields and a non-trivial irreducible representation ρ of its Galois group, the Artin L-function L(s, ρ) extends to an entire function on the whole complex plane.
nodes.by: Emil Artin, 1923, in the paper introducing these L-functions
nodes.note: Langlands (1970) pointed out that it would follow from his reciprocity conjecture. Known for one-dimensional representations, for odd two-dimensional representations over ℚ (from the proof of Serre's modularity conjecture by Khare and Wintenberger, 2009), and for two-dimensional tetrahedral (Langlands 1980) and octahedral (Tunnell 1981) ones. The general icosahedral case is open.

nodes.name: Hodge conjecture
nodes.statement: On a smooth complex projective variety, every rational cohomology class of Hodge type (p, p) is a rational linear combination of classes of algebraic subvarieties.
nodes.by: W. V. D. Hodge, from work in the 1930s, presented at the 1950 International Congress of Mathematicians
nodes.note: A Clay Millennium Prize problem, still unsolved. It implies the Lefschetz and Künneth standard conjectures and standard conjecture D for varieties in characteristic zero.

nodes.name: Lefschetz theorem on (1,1)-classes
nodes.statement: On a smooth complex projective variety, every integral cohomology class of degree 2 and Hodge type (1, 1) is the class of a divisor.
nodes.by: Solomon Lefschetz, 1924
nodes.note: This is the Hodge conjecture in degree 2, proven before the conjecture was stated. Combined with the hard Lefschetz theorem it gives the Hodge conjecture for all varieties of dimension at most three.

nodes.name: Tate conjecture
nodes.statement: For a smooth projective variety over a finitely generated field such as a finite field or a number field, the part of its ℓ-adic cohomology in even degree that is fixed by the Galois group is spanned by classes of algebraic cycles.
nodes.by: John Tate, 1963
nodes.note: Open in general, even for divisors. Proven for divisors on abelian varieties (Tate 1966 over finite fields, Faltings over number fields) and for K3 surfaces. Matt Broe posted a proof for abelian fourfolds over finite fields in August 2026.
nodes.claim: An October 2026 OpenAI catalogue of AI-generated manuscripts claims the Hodge conjecture for CM abelian varieties and, through a theorem of Milne, the Tate conjecture for all abelian varieties over finite fields in every codimension. It has not been independently checked.

nodes.name: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture over function fields
nodes.statement: For the Jacobian of a curve defined over the function field of a curve over a finite field, the rank of its group of rational points equals the order of vanishing of its L-function at s = 1.
nodes.by: John Tate, 1966, carrying the conjecture of Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer to global function fields
nodes.note: For a surface fibred over a curve over a finite field, the Tate conjecture for divisors on the surface is equivalent to this conjecture for the Jacobian of the generic fibre. That is why proofs of the Tate conjecture for special surfaces give BSD for special curves.

nodes.name: Grothendieck's standard conjecture D
nodes.statement: On a smooth projective variety, an algebraic cycle whose intersection number with every other cycle is zero (numerically trivial) also has zero cohomology class (homologically trivial).
nodes.by: Alexander Grothendieck, 1969
nodes.note: The Hodge conjecture and the Tate conjecture each imply it in characteristic zero. Over finite fields the Tate conjecture gives it only together with semisimplicity of Frobenius. Lieberman (1968) proved it over the complex numbers in dimension at most 4 and for abelian varieties.

nodes.name: Grothendieck's Lefschetz standard conjecture (conjecture B)
nodes.statement: On a smooth projective variety of dimension n, the inverse of each hard Lefschetz isomorphism H^i → H^(2n−i) (cupping n − i times with a hyperplane class) is induced by an algebraic cycle on X × X.
nodes.by: Alexander Grothendieck, 1969
nodes.note: Conjecture D implies it, and so does the Tate conjecture. Together with the Hodge standard conjecture, the standard conjectures would make homological and numerical motives agree, giving a semisimple Tannakian category of pure motives, and would have given the Riemann Hypothesis part of the Weil conjectures.

nodes.name: Hironaka's resolution of singularities
nodes.statement: Every algebraic variety over a field of characteristic 0 has a resolution of singularities: a smooth variety with a proper birational map onto it.
nodes.by: Heisuke Hironaka, 1964

nodes.name: Deligne's mixed Hodge structure on smooth varieties
nodes.statement: The cohomology H^n(U, ℤ) of every smooth complex algebraic variety U, compact or not, carries a natural mixed Hodge structure, and maps between varieties respect it.
nodes.by: Pierre Deligne, Théorie de Hodge II, 1971
nodes.note: The construction starts from a good compactification: a smooth complete variety containing U whose boundary is a normal crossings divisor. Such compactifications, and the comparisons that show the result does not depend on the choice, come from resolution of singularities.

nodes.name: Resolution of singularities in positive characteristic
nodes.statement: Every algebraic variety over a field of characteristic p > 0 has a resolution of singularities: a nonsingular (regular) variety with a proper birational map onto it.
nodes.by: Open in general since Hironaka settled characteristic 0 in 1964; surfaces by Shreeram Abhyankar, 1956; threefolds by Abhyankar for characteristic above 5, 1966, and by Vincent Cossart and Olivier Piltant in all characteristics, 2008 and 2009
nodes.note: Open in dimension 4 and higher. The problem is known for many incorrect proofs and announced proofs that never appeared. Aise Johan de Jong's alterations (1996) give a weaker substitute that is enough for many uses.

nodes.name: Feit–Thompson theorem (odd order theorem)
nodes.statement: Every finite group of odd order is solvable. Equivalently, every non-abelian finite simple group has even order.
nodes.by: Walter Feit and John G. Thompson, 1963
nodes.note: Settles a conjecture of Burnside. The 255-page proof was checked by computer in the Coq (now Rocq) proof assistant by Georges Gonthier and colleagues in 2012.

nodes.name: Classification of finite simple groups
nodes.statement: Every finite simple group is a cyclic group of prime order, an alternating group, a group of Lie type, or one of 26 sporadic groups.
nodes.by: Many authors, about 1955 to 2004; the last gap, the quasithin case, was closed by Michael Aschbacher and Stephen D. Smith, 2004
nodes.note: The Feit–Thompson theorem disposes of the groups of odd order, which made the strategy of studying centralizers of involutions possible. A second-generation proof led by Gorenstein, Lyons and Solomon is still being published.

nodes.name: Schreier conjecture
nodes.statement: For every finite simple group G, the outer automorphism group Out(G) is solvable.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Otto Schreier, 1926; proven as a corollary of the classification of finite simple groups
nodes.note: No proof that avoids the classification is known.

nodes.name: Classification of finite 2-transitive permutation groups
nodes.statement: Every finite permutation group that can move any ordered pair of distinct points to any other ordered pair appears on an explicit known list.
nodes.by: William Burnside (every such group is affine or almost simple, 1897); Bertram Huppert (solvable groups, 1957); Christoph Hering (remaining affine groups, completed 1985); almost simple groups by Curtis, Kantor, Seitz and others, using the classification
nodes.note: The almost simple case, and Hering's affine case, use the classification of finite simple groups.

nodes.name: Two-generation of finite simple groups
nodes.statement: Every finite simple group can be generated by two of its elements.
nodes.by: Robert Steinberg (groups of Lie type, 1962); Michael Aschbacher and Robert Guralnick (sporadic groups, 1984)
nodes.note: The proof goes through the list of finite simple groups family by family, so it relies on the classification.

nodes.name: Inverse Galois problem
nodes.statement: Every finite group is the Galois group of some Galois extension of the rational numbers.
nodes.by: Studied systematically since David Hilbert, who realized the symmetric and alternating groups with his irreducibility theorem (1892)
nodes.note: Known for symmetric and alternating groups (Hilbert), solvable groups (Shafarevich) and many simple groups through Thompson's rigidity method. In 2026 Huang, Jackson, Lee, Poonen, Pries and Zhang realized the Mathieu group M23, the last sporadic group that was missing.

nodes.name: Shafarevich's theorem on solvable Galois groups
nodes.statement: Every finite solvable group is the Galois group of some finite extension of the rational numbers.
nodes.by: Igor Shafarevich, 1954; a gap found by Alexander Schmidt was repaired by Shafarevich in 1989

nodes.name: Jacobian conjecture in two variables
nodes.statement: If a polynomial map of the plane, (x, y) ↦ (P(x, y), Q(x, y)) with complex coefficients, has Jacobian determinant equal to a nonzero constant, then it has an inverse that is also given by polynomials.
nodes.by: Ludwig Kraus, 1884 (two variables); Ott-Heinrich Keller, 1939 (any number of variables)
nodes.note: The version in three or more variables is false: Levent Alpöge presented a counterexample in three variables on 19 July 2026, and adding coordinates extends it to all higher dimensions. The two-variable case remains open and has a long history of false proofs.

nodes.name: Dixmier conjecture for the first Weyl algebra
nodes.statement: Over a field of characteristic zero, every endomorphism of the first Weyl algebra A₁ (the algebra generated by x and ∂ with ∂x − x∂ = 1) is an automorphism.
nodes.by: Jacques Dixmier, 1968
nodes.note: The Jacobian conjecture in 2n variables implies the Dixmier conjecture for Aₙ (Tsuchimoto 2005; Belov-Kanel and Kontsevich 2007), so the planar case would settle A₁. For Aₙ with n ≥ 3 the conjecture is false, because Dixmier for Aₙ implies the Jacobian conjecture in n variables. A₂ remains open. Alexander Zheglov announced a proposed proof for A₁ in 2024.

nodes.name: Mordell–Weil theorem
nodes.statement: For an abelian variety A over a number field K, such as an elliptic curve over the rationals, the group A(K) of K-rational points is a finitely generated abelian group.
nodes.by: Louis Mordell, 1922 (elliptic curves over ℚ); André Weil, 1929 (Jacobians over number fields)
nodes.note: The proof has two halves: a descent showing A(K)/2A(K) is finite, and a height argument. The number of generators of infinite order is the rank.

nodes.name: Chabauty's theorem
nodes.statement: If a curve of genus g ≥ 2 over ℚ has a Jacobian whose Mordell–Weil group has rank less than g, the curve has only finitely many rational points.
nodes.by: Claude Chabauty, 1941
nodes.note: It was the main result toward Mordell's conjecture over ℚ before Faltings proved it in 1983. Robert Coleman (1985) turned the method into an explicit bound on the number of rational points.

nodes.name: Jacobson–Morozov theorem
nodes.statement: In a semi-simple Lie algebra over a field of characteristic zero, every nonzero nilpotent element e can be extended to an sl₂-triple: there are elements f and h with [h,e] = 2e, [h,f] = −2f and [e,f] = h.
nodes.by: Morozov, 1942, and Jacobson, 1951
nodes.note: Conversely, the element e of any sl₂-triple is always nilpotent. The theorem also has a form for reductive linear algebraic groups over a field of characteristic zero.

nodes.name: Joubert's theorem
nodes.statement: Let K and L be fields, with L a separable field extension of K of degree 6, and suppose the characteristic of K is not 2. Then L is generated over K by some element λ whose minimal polynomial has the form t⁶ + c₄t⁴ + c₂t² + c₁t + c₀ for some constants c₄, c₂, c₁, c₀ in K.
nodes.by: Charles Joubert, 1867; proved by Daniel F. Coray in 1987 for characteristic neither 2 nor 3
nodes.note: Joubert seems to have assumed that the fields are subfields of the complex numbers. Zinovy Reichstein proved in 2014 that the condition on the characteristic is necessary in general, although the conclusion holds in characteristic 2 under additional assumptions on K and L.

nodes.name: Frattini's argument
nodes.statement: Let G be a finite group with a normal subgroup H, and let P be a Sylow p-subgroup of H. Then G = N_G(P)H, where N_G(P) is the normalizer of P in G and N_G(P)H is the product of the two subsets.
nodes.by: Giovanni Frattini, 1885, who took the argument from a paper of Alfredo Capelli, 1884
nodes.note: Frattini used it when defining the Frattini subgroup of a group. It can be used in a proof that every finite nilpotent group is a direct product of its Sylow subgroups.

nodes.name: Eisenstein's criterion
nodes.statement: Let Q(x) = aₙxⁿ + ... + a₁x + a₀ have integer coefficients. If there is a prime p that divides each aᵢ for 0 ≤ i < n, does not divide aₙ, and whose square does not divide a₀, then Q cannot be written as a product of non-constant polynomials with rational coefficients.
nodes.by: First published in a version by Theodor Schönemann, 1846; Gotthold Eisenstein, after whom it is named, published his version in 1850
nodes.note: The condition is sufficient but not necessary, so it does not detect every irreducible polynomial. It proves that the cyclotomic polynomials for prime numbers are irreducible.

nodes.name: Sylow theorems
nodes.statement: Let G be a finite group, p a prime that divides the order of G, and pⁿ the highest power of p that divides the order of G. Then G has a subgroup of order pⁿ, the subgroups of order pⁿ are exactly the Sylow p-subgroups (the largest subgroups in which every element has an order that is a power of p), any two of them are conjugate, and their number is congruent to 1 mod p and divides the order of G.
nodes.by: Peter Ludwig Sylow, 1872
nodes.note: The theorems give a partial converse to Lagrange's theorem, which says that the order of every subgroup of a finite group divides the order of the group. A weaker version of the first theorem, Cauchy's theorem, was first proved by Augustin-Louis Cauchy.

nodes.name: Golden–Thompson inequality
nodes.statement: For any two real symmetric or complex Hermitian matrices A and B of the same size, the trace of e^(A+B) is at most the trace of e^A·e^B, that is, tr e^(A+B) ≤ tr(e^A e^B).
nodes.by: Proved independently by Golden and by Thompson, 1965
nodes.note: Equality holds only when A and B commute, as Petz proved in 1994. The inequality has been generalized to three and more Hermitian matrices.

nodes.name: Snake lemma
nodes.statement: In an abelian category, such as abelian groups or vector spaces, take a commutative diagram with exact rows A → B → C → 0 (maps f, g) and 0 → A′ → B′ → C′ (maps f′, g′), joined by vertical maps a: A → A′, b: B → B′, c: C → C′. Then there is an exact sequence ker f → ker a → ker b → ker c → coker a → coker b → coker c → coker g′, whose map d from ker c to coker a is called the connecting homomorphism.
nodes.note: It is used to construct long exact sequences in homological algebra and algebraic topology. In the category of groups, with cokernels taken as quotients by normal closures, the resulting sequence can fail to be exact.

nodes.name: Hilbert's Nullstellensatz
nodes.statement: Let k be a field, K an algebraically closed field extension of k, and J an ideal in the polynomial ring k[X₁, …, Xₙ]. If a polynomial p in k[X₁, …, Xₙ] vanishes at every point of Kⁿ where all polynomials of J vanish, then pʳ belongs to J for some natural number r.
nodes.by: David Hilbert, 1893
nodes.note: In the weak form, a system of polynomial equations over an algebraically closed field has no solution exactly when 1 = g₁f₁ + … + gₘfₘ for some polynomials gᵢ. The theorem relates geometry and algebra.

nodes.name: Polynomial remainder theorem
nodes.statement: For every number r, any polynomial f(x) of degree n ≥ 1 equals f(r) plus the product of x − r and a polynomial of degree n − 1. So f(r) is the remainder of the Euclidean division of f(x) by x − r, and x − r divides f(x) if and only if f(r) = 0.
nodes.by: Named after Étienne Bézout (little Bézout's theorem)
nodes.note: The last part, that x − r divides f(x) exactly when f(r) = 0, is known as the factor theorem.

nodes.name: Bergman's diamond lemma
nodes.statement: Let k be a commutative ring with identity, and let elements g_σ = w_σ − f_σ generate a two-sided ideal I of the free associative algebra k⟨X⟩. Here w_σ is the leading word of g_σ under a fixed admissible ordering of the words, and f_σ is a combination of smaller words. Then the following are equivalent: all overlap and inclusion ambiguities among the g_σ are resolvable; every element of k⟨X⟩ is reduction-unique; the images in k⟨X⟩/I of the reduced words (words containing no w_σ) form a k-basis.
nodes.by: Named after George Bergman
nodes.note: It extends Gröbner bases to non-commutative rings. Its proof gives an algorithm for finding a non-commutative Gröbner basis, and unlike Buchberger's algorithm this one may not terminate.

nodes.name: Švarc–Milnor lemma
nodes.statement: Let G be a group acting by isometries on a proper length space X so that the action is properly discontinuous and cocompact. Then G is finitely generated, and for every finite generating set S of G and every point p in X, the orbit map g ↦ gp from G with the word metric d_S to X is a quasi-isometry.
nodes.by: Goes back to Albert S. Schwarz, 1955, and John Milnor, 1968
nodes.note: Pierre de la Harpe called it the fundamental observation in geometric group theory. One consequence is that for every n ≥ 1 the group ℤⁿ is quasi-isometric to ℝⁿ.

nodes.name: Factor theorem
nodes.statement: Let f(x) be a polynomial in one variable with coefficients in a commutative ring, for example a field, and let a be an element of that ring. Then x − a is a factor of f(x) if and only if f(a) = 0.
nodes.note: It is a special case of the polynomial remainder theorem. It shows that factoring a polynomial and finding its roots are essentially equivalent problems.

nodes.name: Local invariant cycle theorem
nodes.statement: Let p be a surjective proper map from a Kähler manifold X to the unit disk that has maximal rank everywhere except over 0. Then every cohomology class on a fibre p⁻¹(t), t ≠ 0, that is invariant under the circle (monodromy) action is the restriction of a cohomology class on all of X. In short, H*(X) → H*(p⁻¹(t))^{S¹} is surjective.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Griffiths; first proved by Clemens
nodes.note: The theorem is also a consequence of the BBD decomposition. Deligne proved an analogous surjectivity statement for proper morphisms over the henselization of k[T] with k algebraically closed.

nodes.name: Gamas's theorem
nodes.statement: Let V be a finite-dimensional complex vector space, λ a partition of n, and χ^λ the character of the corresponding irreducible representation of the symmetric group S_n. The tensor v_1 ⊗ … ⊗ v_n symmetrized by χ^λ, namely (χ^λ(e)/n!) ∑ χ^λ(σ) v_σ(1) ⊗ … ⊗ v_σ(n) summed over all σ in S_n with e the identity, is nonzero if and only if the vectors v_i can be partitioned into linearly independent sets whose sizes match the lengths of the columns of λ.
nodes.by: Carlos Gamas, 1988
nodes.note: Additional proofs have been given by Pate and Berget.

nodes.name: Cauchy's theorem
nodes.statement: If G is a finite group and p is a prime number dividing the number of elements of G, then G contains an element of order p, that is, an element x with xᵖ = e and xʲ ≠ e for 0 < j < p.
nodes.by: Augustin-Louis Cauchy, 1845
nodes.note: It is a partial converse to Lagrange's theorem and is generalized by Sylow's first theorem.

nodes.name: Hurwitz's theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be a finite-dimensional real algebra with a unit element, not necessarily associative, with a nondegenerate positive-definite quadratic form q that is multiplicative on nonzero elements, so q(ab) = q(a)q(b). Then A is isomorphic to the real numbers, the complex numbers, the quaternions or the octonions, and there are no other possibilities.
nodes.by: Adolf Hurwitz, published posthumously in 1923
nodes.note: It implies that multiplicative formulas for sums of squares can only occur in 1, 2, 4 and 8 dimensions, a result Hurwitz originally proved in 1898.

nodes.name: Mitchell's embedding theorem
nodes.statement: If A is a small abelian category, then there is a ring R (with 1, not necessarily commutative) and a full, faithful and exact functor F from A to the category R-Mod of all left R-modules.
nodes.by: Named after Barry Mitchell and Peter Freyd
nodes.note: It lets one use element-wise diagram chasing proofs in abelian categories. Also called the Freyd–Mitchell theorem or the full embedding theorem.

nodes.name: Euler's four-square identity
nodes.statement: For any two quadruples (a₁, a₂, a₃, a₄) and (b₁, b₂, b₃, b₄) from a commutative ring, (a₁² + a₂² + a₃² + a₄²)(b₁² + b₂² + b₃² + b₄²) = (a₁b₁ − a₂b₂ − a₃b₃ − a₄b₄)² + (a₁b₂ + a₂b₁ + a₃b₄ − a₄b₃)² + (a₁b₃ − a₂b₄ + a₃b₁ + a₄b₂)² + (a₁b₄ + a₂b₃ − a₃b₂ + a₄b₁)². So the product of two sums of four squares is itself a sum of four squares.
nodes.by: Euler, in a letter to Goldbach dated May 4, 1748
nodes.note: Lagrange used the identity to prove his four square theorem. For real numbers it says that the absolute value of a product of two quaternions is the product of their absolute values.

nodes.name: Jacobi identity
nodes.statement: In any associative algebra, for example the n×n matrices, the commutator [X,Y] = XY − YX satisfies [X,[Y,Z]] + [Y,[Z,X]] + [Z,[X,Y]] = 0 for all elements X, Y, Z.
nodes.by: Named after Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi, who derived it for Poisson brackets in his 1862 paper on differential equations
nodes.note: The cross product of vectors and the Poisson brackets of analytical mechanics satisfy the same identity. In a Lie algebra it says that the action of any element on the algebra is a derivation.

nodes.name: Bogomolov–Sommese vanishing theorem
nodes.statement: Let (X, D) be a complex projective snc pair, that is, a smooth complex projective variety X with a simple normal crossing divisor D, and let A be an invertible sheaf (line bundle) on X whose Kodaira–Iitaka dimension κ(A) is greater than p. Then the space of global sections H⁰(X, A⁻¹ ⊗ Ωᵖ_X(log D)) is zero.
nodes.by: Named after Fedor Bogomolov and Andrew Sommese
nodes.note: The theorem has differing versions, and this vanishing of a cohomology group is equivalent to them. The vanishing is why it is called a vanishing theorem.

nodes.name: Hajós's theorem
nodes.statement: Suppose a finite abelian group is written as a product of sets of the form {e, a, a², …, a^(s−1)}, where e is the identity element, so that every element of the group arises in exactly one way by multiplying one element from each set. Then at least one of these sets is a subgroup.
nodes.by: György Hajós, 1941; an equivalent statement on homogeneous linear forms was conjectured earlier by Hermann Minkowski
nodes.note: Hajós proved it using group rings, and Rédei later proved it when the factors only need to contain the identity and have prime cardinality. A consequence is Minkowski's conjecture that in any lattice tiling of space by cubes, two cubes meet face to face.

nodes.name: Degen's eight-square identity
nodes.statement: For any numbers a₁, …, a₈ and b₁, …, b₈, the product (a₁² + … + a₈²)(b₁² + … + b₈²) equals a sum of eight squares. Each of these is the square of an explicit sum of the products aᵢbⱼ with fixed signs, the first being (a₁b₁ − a₂b₂ − a₃b₃ − a₄b₄ − a₅b₅ − a₆b₆ − a₇b₇ − a₈b₈)², so the product of two sums of eight squares is again a sum of eight squares.
nodes.by: First discovered by Carl Ferdinand Degen around 1818; independently rediscovered by John Thomas Graves, 1843, and Arthur Cayley, 1845
nodes.note: In algebraic terms it says that the norm of a product of two octonions equals the product of their norms. In 1898 Adolf Hurwitz proved that no similar bilinear identity exists for any number of squares other than 1, 2, 4 and 8.

nodes.name: Fundamental theorem on homomorphisms
nodes.statement: Let f: G → H be a group homomorphism and N a normal subgroup of G contained in the kernel of f. Then there is exactly one homomorphism h: G/N → H with f = h ∘ φ, where φ: G → G/N is the natural projection, and h is injective if and only if N equals the kernel of f.
nodes.by: Dates back to Richard Dedekind; further formalized by Emmy Noether into the isomorphism theorems
nodes.note: Taking N to be the kernel of f gives the first isomorphism theorem: every homomorphic image of a group is isomorphic to a quotient group.

nodes.name: Nagata's compactification theorem
nodes.statement: Every abstract variety can be embedded in a complete variety. More generally, every separated morphism of finite type to a Noetherian scheme S can be written as an open immersion followed by a proper morphism.
nodes.by: Introduced by Nagata
nodes.note: Deligne showed that the condition that S is Noetherian can be replaced by the weaker condition that S is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. The theorem is used to define the algebraic-geometry analogue of cohomology with compact support.

nodes.name: Forster–Swan theorem
nodes.statement: Let M be a finitely generated module over a commutative Noetherian ring R with identity. For each prime ideal 𝔭 of R, let b(𝔭) be the minimal number of generators of the localization M_𝔭 plus the dimension of R/𝔭. Then the minimal number of generators of M is at most the supremum of b(𝔭) over all prime ideals 𝔭 with M_𝔭 ≠ 0.
nodes.by: Otto Forster, 1964 (in a more restrictive form); generalized by Richard G. Swan, 1967
nodes.note: The bound needs only the minimal number of generators of the localizations of M.

nodes.name: Stein–Rosenberg theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be a real n×n matrix with aᵢⱼ ≤ 0 for i ≠ j and aᵢᵢ > 0 for all i, and let T_J and T₁ be the iteration matrices of the Jacobi method and the Gauss-Seidel method for A. Then exactly one of these holds, where ρ is the spectral radius: ρ(T_J) = ρ(T₁) = 0; or 0 < ρ(T₁) < ρ(T_J) < 1; or ρ(T_J) = ρ(T₁) = 1; or 1 < ρ(T_J) < ρ(T₁).
nodes.note: So the two methods either both converge or both diverge, and when they converge Gauss-Seidel is asymptotically faster. The proof uses the Perron-Frobenius theorem for non-negative matrices.

nodes.name: Lagrange's identity
nodes.statement: For any numbers a₁,…,aₙ and b₁,…,bₙ that are real or complex, or more generally elements of a commutative ring, (a₁² + … + aₙ²)(b₁² + … + bₙ²) − (a₁b₁ + … + aₙbₙ)² equals the sum of (aᵢbⱼ − aⱼbᵢ)² over all pairs i < j. For complex numbers there is also a form with absolute values: (∑|aₖ|²)(∑|bₖ|²) − |∑aₖbₖ|² equals the sum of |aᵢb̄ⱼ − aⱼb̄ᵢ|² over all pairs i < j.
nodes.by: Named after Joseph Louis Lagrange
nodes.note: It generalises the Brahmagupta–Fibonacci identity and is a special form of the Binet–Cauchy identity. Because the right-hand side is non-negative, it implies Cauchy's inequality in ℝⁿ and ℂⁿ.

nodes.name: Nielsen–Schreier theorem
nodes.statement: Every subgroup of a free group is itself a free group. If G is a free group of rank n and H is a subgroup of finite index e, then H is free of rank 1 + e(n−1).
nodes.by: Jakob Nielsen proved the case of finitely generated subgroups, 1921; Otto Schreier proved the full theorem, 1926
nodes.note: It is a non-abelian analogue of an older result of Richard Dedekind, that every subgroup of a free abelian group is free abelian.

nodes.name: Nadel vanishing theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a smooth complex projective variety with canonical divisor K_X, D an effective ℚ-divisor and L a line bundle on X, and let 𝒥(D) be the multiplier ideal sheaf of D. If L − D is big and nef, then the cohomology group Hⁱ(X, O_X(K_X + L) ⊗ 𝒥(D)) is zero for every i > 0.
nodes.by: A. M. Nadel, 1989
nodes.note: It generalizes the Kodaira vanishing theorem using singular metrics with strictly positive curvature, and can be seen as an analytical analogue of the Kawamata–Viehweg vanishing theorem.

nodes.name: Noether normalization lemma
nodes.statement: For any field k and any finitely generated commutative k-algebra A, there are elements y₁, …, y_d in A that are algebraically independent over k and such that A is a finitely generated module over the polynomial ring k[y₁, …, y_d]. The integer d equals the Krull dimension of A, and if A is an integral domain, d is also the transcendence degree over k of the field of fractions of A.
nodes.by: Emmy Noether, 1926
nodes.note: Geometrically, any affine variety is a branched covering of affine space. The lemma yields Zariski's lemma as a corollary, which in turn gives a proof of Hilbert's Nullstellensatz.

nodes.name: Brauer's height zero conjecture
nodes.statement: Let G be a finite group, p a prime and B a Brauer p-block of G with defect group D. Every irreducible complex character χ in B has height zero, meaning that the power of p dividing χ(1) equals the power of p dividing the index |G:D|, if and only if D is abelian.
nodes.by: Formulated by Richard Brauer, 1955; the 'if' direction proved by Radha Kessar and Gunter Malle, 2013; proof completed by Gunter Malle, Gabriel Navarro, A. A. Schaeffer Fry and Pham Huu Tiep, 2024
nodes.note: It is Problem 23 in Brauer's list of problems. Solving it for blocks whose defect groups are Sylow p-subgroups also solves Brauer's Problem 12.

nodes.name: Brauer's k(B) conjecture
nodes.statement: Let G be a finite group, p a prime and B a p-block of G with defect group D. Then the number of irreducible complex characters in B is at most the order of D.
nodes.by: Richard Brauer, first announced 1946
nodes.note: It is Problem 20 in Brauer's list of problems. For blocks of p-solvable groups it is equivalent to the k(GV) problem, which was proved by John Thompson and Geoffrey Robinson except for finitely many primes, with the last cases published in 2004.

nodes.name: Burnside's lemma
nodes.statement: Let G be a finite group acting on a set X. Then the number of orbits equals the average, over all elements g of G, of the number of points of X fixed by g: |X/G| = (1/|G|) ∑_{g ∈ G} |X^g|.
nodes.by: Known to Augustin Louis Cauchy in 1845 and to Ferdinand Georg Frobenius in 1887; William Burnside stated and proved it in his 1897 book on finite groups
nodes.note: It is used to count distinct objects up to a symmetry, treating objects that are symmetric to each other as the same.

nodes.name: Bruguières modularity theorem
nodes.statement: A pre-modular tensor category has non-degenerate braiding if and only if its modular S-matrix is invertible.
nodes.by: Alain Bruguières, 2000
nodes.note: It shows that two formulations of the modularity condition of a modular tensor category are equivalent.

nodes.name: Schauenburg–Ng theorem
nodes.statement: For every modular tensor category, the kernel of its modular group representation is a congruence subgroup of SL₂(ℤ). Since congruence subgroups have finite index in SL₂(ℤ), every such modular representation has finite image.
nodes.by: Conjectured since 1987 by Greg Moore and others; proved by Siu-Hung Ng and Peter Schauenburg, 2010
nodes.note: The conjecture came from conformal field theory. The proof introduced generalised Frobenius–Schur indicators, which have found separate applications in mathematical physics.

nodes.name: 2-Yoneda lemma
nodes.statement: Let F be a contravariant pseudofunctor on a category C and let x be an object of C. Then evaluation at the identity is an equivalence of categories from the category of natural transformations from h_x = Hom(−, x) to F onto F(x).
nodes.note: It generalizes the Yoneda lemma to 2-categories. The coherence theorem for bicategories follows from it.

nodes.name: Joyal's extension theorem
nodes.statement: Let C be a quasicategory and u: X → Y a morphism of C. Then u is an isomorphism if and only if, for every n ≥ 2, every map of simplicial sets Λⁿ₀ → C whose initial edge is u extends to an n-simplex Δⁿ → C. This is also equivalent to the same extension property for every map Λⁿₙ → C whose edge from vertex n−1 to vertex n is u.
nodes.by: André Joyal
nodes.note: In higher category theory it proves the statement that an ∞-groupoid is a Kan complex, a version of the homotopy hypothesis.

nodes.name: Frobenius theorem
nodes.statement: Every finite-dimensional associative division algebra over the real numbers is isomorphic to ℝ (the real numbers), ℂ (the complex numbers) or ℍ (the quaternions).
nodes.by: Ferdinand Georg Frobenius, 1877
nodes.note: These three algebras have real dimension 1, 2 and 4. ℝ and ℂ are commutative, but ℍ is not.

nodes.name: Hadamard's inequality
nodes.statement: For a square matrix N with complex entries and columns v₁, …, vₙ, the absolute value of the determinant of N is at most the product of the lengths of the columns. If the columns are all non-zero, equality holds if and only if they are orthogonal.
nodes.by: Jacques Hadamard, 1893
nodes.note: For real matrices it bounds the volume marked out by n vectors in n-dimensional Euclidean space by the product of their lengths. Matrices of +1 and −1 entries that reach the bound are called Hadamard matrices.

nodes.name: Pasting theorem
nodes.statement: Every 2-pasting diagram in a strict 2-category, and also in a weak 2-category, has a unique composite: all the orders in which its 2-cells can be composed give the same 2-cell.
nodes.by: Proved for strict 2-categories by Power, 1990, and for weak 2-categories by Verity, 1992 (thesis); pasting first appeared in Bénabou, 1967
nodes.note: Versions exist for Gray-categories and for strict n-categories, proved by Johnson, 1989 and Power, 1991, with a different definition of pasting scheme.

nodes.name: Descartes's rule of signs
nodes.statement: For a single-variable polynomial with real coefficients, the number of positive roots, with a root of multiplicity k counted k times, is either equal to the number of sign changes in the sequence of its nonzero coefficients or less than it by an even number. In particular, if there are zero or one sign changes, the number of positive roots equals the number of sign changes.
nodes.by: René Descartes
nodes.note: Applying the rule after a linear fractional transformation counts roots in any interval, which is the basic idea of Budan's theorem and is used in the fastest algorithms for isolating real roots.

nodes.name: Nakayama's lemma
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative ring with identity, I an ideal of R, and M a finitely generated R-module. If IM = M, then there is an r in R with r ≡ 1 (mod I) such that rM = 0; in particular, if J(R) is the Jacobson radical of R and J(R)M = M, then M = 0.
nodes.by: Named after Tadashi Nakayama, who introduced it in its present form in 1951; first discovered in the special case of ideals in a commutative ring by Wolfgang Krull and then in general by Goro Azumaya, 1951
nodes.note: It gives a precise sense in which finitely generated modules over a commutative ring behave like vector spaces over a field. In the commutative case it follows from a generalized form of the Cayley–Hamilton theorem.

nodes.name: Hilbert's Theorem 90
nodes.statement: Let L/K be an extension of fields whose Galois group G = Gal(L/K) is cyclic of order n and generated by an element σ. If an element a of L has relative norm N(a) = a·σ(a)·σ²(a)···σⁿ⁻¹(a) = 1, then there is an element b in L such that a = b/σ(b).
nodes.by: Originally due to Kummer; named for being the 90th theorem in David Hilbert's Zahlbericht, 1897
nodes.note: It leads to Kummer theory. Noether (1933) gave a more general form: for a finite Galois extension L/K with Galois group G, the first cohomology group H¹(G, L^×) is trivial.

nodes.name: Spectral theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be a Hermitian (self-adjoint) linear map on a finite-dimensional complex inner product space, for example a Hermitian matrix or a real symmetric matrix. Then all eigenvalues of A are real, and the space has an orthonormal basis made of eigenvectors of A, so A is represented by a diagonal matrix in that basis.
nodes.by: Augustin-Louis Cauchy proved it for real symmetric matrices; generalized by John von Neumann
nodes.note: The same holds for normal matrices, where the eigenvalues need not be real, and for compact self-adjoint operators on Hilbert spaces. For bounded self-adjoint operators, which may have no eigenvectors, the theorem says the operator is unitarily equivalent to a multiplication operator.

nodes.name: Five lemma
nodes.statement: In an abelian category (such as abelian groups or vector spaces over a field) or in the category of groups, take a commutative diagram with two exact rows A → B → C → D → E and A′ → B′ → C′ → D′ → E′ joined by vertical maps l: A → A′, m: B → B′, n: C → C′, p: D → D′, q: E → E′. If m and p are isomorphisms, l is an epimorphism and q is a monomorphism, then n is also an isomorphism.
nodes.note: It combines two four lemmas, which are dual to each other. It is often applied to long exact sequences in homology and cohomology, for example to show that two cohomology theories of the same object agree.

nodes.name: Pfister's sixteen-square identity
nodes.statement: (x₁²+…+x₁₆²)(y₁²+…+y₁₆²) = z₁²+…+z₁₆², where each zᵢ is linear in the y's and a rational function of the x's with denominator x₁²+…+x₈², so the identity holds whenever x₁, …, x₈ are not all zero. Thus the product of two sums of sixteen squares is a sum of sixteen squares of rational expressions.
nodes.by: H. Zassenhaus and W. Eichhorn in the 1960s, and independently Albrecht Pfister around the same time
nodes.note: Setting every x and y with index above 8 to zero gives Degen's eight-square identity. By Hurwitz's theorem no sixteen-square identity with bilinear z's exists.

nodes.name: Bézout's theorem
nodes.statement: If two plane projective curves of degrees d₁ and d₂ have no component in common, they meet in exactly d₁d₂ points, counted with multiplicity, including points at infinity and points with coordinates in an algebraically closed field such as the complex numbers. More generally, n projective hypersurfaces in n-dimensional projective space over an algebraically closed field, defined by homogeneous polynomials in n + 1 variables of degrees d₁, …, dₙ, have either infinitely many common points or exactly d₁⋯dₙ common points counted with multiplicity.
nodes.by: Essentially stated by Isaac Newton, 1687, who had stated it as early as 1665; the general theorem was published by Étienne Bézout, 1779; Jean-Pierre Serre's algebraic definition of multiplicity, 1958, led to a proof valid over any algebraically closed field
nodes.note: If multiplicities and points at infinity are not counted, it gives only an upper bound on the number of points, called the Bézout bound.

nodes.name: Woodbury matrix identity
nodes.statement: Let A be an n×n matrix, U an n×k matrix, C a k×k matrix and V a k×n matrix, where A, C and C⁻¹ + VA⁻¹U are invertible. Then A + UCV is invertible and (A + UCV)⁻¹ = A⁻¹ − A⁻¹U(C⁻¹ + VA⁻¹U)⁻¹VA⁻¹, so the inverse of a rank-k correction of a matrix is a rank-k correction of the inverse.
nodes.by: Named after Max A. Woodbury; the identity appeared in several papers before the Woodbury report
nodes.note: It is also called the matrix inversion lemma or the Sherman–Morrison–Woodbury formula. It allows efficient computation of inverses and of solutions to linear systems after low-rank modifications, for example in the Kalman filter.

nodes.name: Perron–Frobenius theorem
nodes.statement: If every entry of a real square matrix A is positive, then A has a positive real eigenvalue r that is a simple root of its characteristic polynomial, every other eigenvalue (possibly complex) has absolute value strictly less than r, and r has an eigenvector whose components are all positive. If A is only non-negative but irreducible, r is still a positive simple eigenvalue with an all-positive eigenvector, but exactly h eigenvalues have absolute value r, where h is the period of A.
nodes.by: Proved in its first part by Perron, 1907, and extended by Frobenius, 1912
nodes.note: It has applications to Markov chains, dynamical systems, economics, demography and Internet search engines (PageRank).

nodes.name: Hua's identity
nodes.statement: For any elements a and b of a division ring with ab ≠ 0 and ab ≠ 1, a − (a⁻¹ + (b⁻¹ − a)⁻¹)⁻¹ = aba.
nodes.by: Named after Hua Luogeng
nodes.note: It is used in a proof of Hua's theorem, which says that an additive map between division rings that sends 1 to 1 and preserves inverses is a homomorphism or an antihomomorphism.

nodes.name: Lawvere's fixed-point theorem
nodes.statement: In a Cartesian closed category, let B be an object. If there is a weakly point-surjective morphism f from some object A to the exponential object B^A, then every endomorphism g: B → B has a fixed point, that is, a morphism b: 1 → B from the terminal object 1 with g ∘ b = b.
nodes.by: William Lawvere, 1969
nodes.note: It is a broad abstract generalization of many diagonal arguments, such as Cantor's diagonal argument, Russell's paradox, Gödel's first incompleteness theorem and Tarski's undefinability theorem.

nodes.name: Jacobson's conjecture
nodes.statement: In a ring that is Noetherian on both the left and the right, the intersection of all the powers Jⁿ of the Jacobson radical J is {0}.
nodes.by: Nathan Jacobson, 1956, in a first version for one-sided Noetherian rings; reformulated for two-sided Noetherian rings after counterexamples by Israel Nathan Herstein, 1965, and Arun Vinayak Jategaonkar
nodes.note: It has only been proven for special types of Noetherian rings. Examples show it can fail when the ring is Noetherian on one side only.

nodes.name: Jordan–Chevalley decomposition
nodes.statement: Let x be a linear operator on a finite-dimensional vector space over a field K whose minimal polynomial is a product of separable polynomials (this always holds when K is a perfect field). Then x can be written in exactly one way as x = xₛ + xₙ, where xₛ is potentially diagonalisable (diagonalisable over some larger field), xₙ is nilpotent and xₛxₙ = xₙxₛ, and both parts are polynomials in x.
nodes.by: Named after Camille Jordan and Claude Chevalley
nodes.note: It generalises the Jordan normal form and exists under weaker hypotheses. Without the condition on the minimal polynomial the decomposition may fail to exist, which can happen over fields that are not perfect.

nodes.name: Bloch's formula
nodes.statement: For every smooth variety X over a field and every q, the Chow group CH^q(X) is isomorphic to the sheaf cohomology group H^q(X, K_q(𝒪_X)), where K_q(𝒪_X) is the sheaf associated to the presheaf U ↦ K_q(U) on the Zariski open subsets U of X.
nodes.by: Introduced by Spencer Bloch for K₂; the general case is due to Quillen
nodes.note: For q = 1 it recovers Pic(X) = H¹(X, 𝒪_X*). The formula for mixed characteristic is still open.

nodes.name: Mautner's lemma
nodes.statement: Let G be a topological group and π a unitary representation of G on a Hilbert space H. If x in G has conjugates yxy⁻¹ converging to the identity element e along a net of elements y, then every vector v of H that is invariant under all the π(y) is also invariant under π(x).
nodes.by: Named after the Austrian-American mathematician Friederich Mautner

nodes.name: Whitehead's lemma
nodes.statement: Let 𝔤 be a finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra over a field of characteristic zero, V a finite-dimensional module over it, and f: 𝔤 → V a linear map with f([x, y]) = x·f(y) − y·f(x) for all x, y. Then there is a vector v in V such that f(x) = x·v for every x in 𝔤; equivalently, the first cohomology group H¹(𝔤, V) is 0.
nodes.by: Named after J. H. C. Whitehead
nodes.note: This first lemma is an important step toward the proof of Weyl's theorem on complete reducibility. Whitehead's second lemma states that under the same conditions H²(𝔤, V) = 0 as well.

nodes.name: Hilbert–Mumford criterion
nodes.statement: Let a reductive group G act linearly on a vector space V and let x be a non-zero point of V. Then x is semi-stable (0 is not in the closure of its orbit) if and only if, for every 1-parameter subgroup of G, x has both a non-positive and a non-negative weight; and x is stable (its orbit is closed and its stabilizer finite) if and only if, for every 1-parameter subgroup of G, x has both a positive and a negative weight.
nodes.by: Introduced by David Hilbert and David Mumford
nodes.note: It shows that the case of the multiplicative group is the typical situation. In moduli problems it shows, for example, that a plane cubic is stable exactly when it is smooth.

nodes.name: Brahmagupta's identity
nodes.statement: For given n, the product of two numbers of the form a² + nb² is again of that form: (a² + nb²)(c² + nd²) = (ac ± nbd)² + n(ad ∓ bc)². The identity holds in the integers, in the rational numbers, and more generally in any commutative ring.
nodes.by: Brahmagupta (598–668), who generalized the Brahmagupta–Fibonacci identity found in Diophantus' Arithmetica (III, 19); the identity later appeared in Fibonacci's Book of Squares in 1225
nodes.note: Brahmagupta used it in his study of what is now called Pell's equation, and Bhaskara II's chakravala method of 1150 for solving that equation was also based on it.

nodes.name: Chebotarev theorem on roots of unity
nodes.statement: Let n be a prime number and let Ω be the n×n matrix with entries ω^(ij) for 1 ≤ i, j ≤ n, where ω = e^(2πi/n). Then every minor of Ω is non-zero.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Ostrowski; first proved by Chebotarev in the 1930s; also discovered independently by Dieudonné
nodes.note: Equivalently, every square submatrix of a DFT matrix of prime length is invertible. Terence Tao used it to extend the uncertainty principle in signal processing.

nodes.name: Fundamental theorem of algebraic K-theory
nodes.statement: Let R be a regular noetherian ring and t a variable. For every i ≥ 0, K_i(R[t]) ≅ K_i(R); for every i ≥ 1, K_i(R[t,t⁻¹]) ≅ K_i(R) ⊕ K_{i−1}(R); and in degree zero, K_0(R[t,t⁻¹]) ≅ K_0(R).
nodes.by: First established in low degrees by Hyman Bass, then extended to higher algebraic K-groups by Daniel Quillen
nodes.note: It describes how K-groups behave when passing from a ring to a polynomial ring or a Laurent polynomial ring. The corresponding results for the G-theory of noetherian rings do not require regularity.

nodes.name: Golod–Shafarevich theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be the free algebra over a field K in n = d+1 non-commuting variables, and let J be the two-sided ideal generated by homogeneous elements f_j of degree d_j, where 2 ≤ d_1 ≤ d_2 ≤ … and d_j tends to infinity. Let r_i be the number of d_j equal to i, let B = A/J and b_j = dim B_j. Then b_j ≥ n·b_{j−1} − ∑ b_{j−i}·r_i, the sum over i from 2 to j, for all j. As a consequence, B is infinite-dimensional if r_i ≤ d²/4 for all i ≥ 2.
nodes.by: Evgeny Golod and Igor Shafarevich, 1964
nodes.note: It solves the class field tower problem by showing that class field towers can be infinite.

nodes.name: Grushko theorem
nodes.statement: If A and B are finitely generated groups, then the rank of their free product A∗B equals rank(A) + rank(B). Here the rank of a group is the smallest number of elements that generate it.
nodes.by: Grushko, 1940; independently Neumann, 1943
nodes.note: Its consequence, the Grushko decomposition theorem, splits every nontrivial finitely generated group into a free product of freely indecomposable factors and a free group.

nodes.name: Hautus lemma
nodes.statement: For a real n×n matrix A and a real n×m matrix B, the following are equivalent: the pair (A, B) is controllable; for every complex number λ the matrix [λI − A, B] has rank n; for every complex number λ that is an eigenvalue of A the matrix [λI − A, B] has rank n. Here [λI − A, B] is the n×(n+m) matrix formed by placing B to the right of λI − A.
nodes.by: A special case first appeared in a paper by Elmer G. Gilbert, 1963; expanded to the current test with contributions by Vasile M. Popov, 1966, Vitold Belevitch, 1968, and Malo Hautus, 1969
nodes.note: It is also known as the Popov-Belevitch-Hautus or PBH test. Analogous forms characterize stabilizability, observability and detectability.

nodes.name: Akizuki–Hopkins–Levitzki theorem
nodes.statement: Let R be a semiprimary ring, that is, a ring with 1 such that R/J(R) is semisimple and the Jacobson radical J(R) is a nilpotent ideal. Then for every R-module M, the three conditions Noetherian, Artinian and having a composition series are equivalent.
nodes.by: Charles Hopkins and Jacob Levitzki, 1939; Yasuo Akizuki proved it for commutative rings in 1935
nodes.note: A direct corollary is that a right Artinian ring is also right Noetherian. Without the semiprimary condition, a module has a composition series if and only if it is both Noetherian and Artinian.

nodes.name: Higman's embedding theorem
nodes.statement: Every finitely generated recursively presented group can be embedded as a subgroup of some finitely presented group.
nodes.by: Graham Higman, 1960s
nodes.note: It implies that there is a universal finitely presented group containing all finitely presented groups as subgroups. It also implies the Novikov-Boone theorem on the existence of a finitely presented group with undecidable word problem.

nodes.name: Weyl's theorem on complete reducibility
nodes.statement: Let 𝔤 be a semisimple Lie algebra over a field of characteristic zero. Then every finite-dimensional module over 𝔤 is semisimple, that is, a direct sum of simple modules.
nodes.by: Weyl, whose original proof for complex semisimple Lie algebras was analytic
nodes.note: It is equivalent to the statement that the enveloping algebra of a finite-dimensional representation is a semisimple ring. Weyl's original proof used the unitarian trick.

nodes.name: Appell–Humbert theorem
nodes.statement: Let T = V/Λ be a complex torus, with Λ a lattice in a complex vector space V. Every line bundle on T arises from a unique pair (H, α), where H is a Hermitian form on V whose imaginary part E is integral on Λ×Λ, and α is a map from Λ to the unit circle with α(u+v) = e^(iπE(u,v)) α(u) α(v); the line bundle is the one defined by the 1-cocycle α(u) e^(πH(z,u) + H(u,u)π/2).
nodes.by: Appell, 1891, and Humbert, 1893, for 2-dimensional tori; Lefschetz, 1921, in general
nodes.note: It describes the line bundles on a complex torus or complex abelian variety. Lefschetz proved that the line bundle is ample exactly when H is positive definite.

nodes.name: Zariski's connectedness theorem
nodes.statement: Let f be a proper surjective morphism of varieties from X to Y such that the function field of Y is separably closed in that of X. Then the inverse image of any normal point of Y is connected.
nodes.by: Oscar Zariski
nodes.note: It extends Zariski's main theorem to morphisms that need not be birational. It gives a rigorous version of Enriques's "principle of degeneration".

nodes.name: Behrend's trace formula
nodes.statement: For a smooth algebraic stack X of finite type over a finite field 𝔽_q, the number of points #X(𝔽_q), where each isomorphism class p is counted with weight 1/#Aut(p), equals q^(dim X) ∑ (−1)^i tr(φ⁻¹; H^i(X, ℚ_l)), the sum running over i ≥ 0. Here φ⁻¹ is the arithmetic Frobenius, the inverse of the geometric Frobenius, and the cohomology is taken in the smooth topology.
nodes.by: Kai Behrend, conjectured 1993, proven 2003
nodes.note: It generalizes the Grothendieck–Lefschetz trace formula and counts points in the stacky way, taking nontrivial automorphisms into account.

nodes.name: Jacobson density theorem
nodes.statement: Let U be a simple right module over a ring R, let D = End_R(U) be the ring of R-module endomorphisms of U (a division ring), and let X ⊂ U be a finite set that is linearly independent over D. Then for every D-linear transformation A on U there is an element r ∈ R with A(x) = x·r for all x in X.
nodes.by: Nathan Jacobson, 1945
nodes.note: It shows that any primitive ring can be viewed as a dense subring of the ring of linear transformations of a vector space. It can be viewed as a generalization of the conclusion of the Artin–Wedderburn theorem about simple Artinian rings.

nodes.name: Keel–Mori theorem
nodes.statement: Let all algebraic spaces be of finite type over a locally Noetherian base, and let j: R → X×X be a flat groupoid whose stabilizer j⁻¹Δ is finite over X, where Δ is the diagonal of X×X. Then there is an algebraic space that is a geometric and uniform categorical quotient of X by j, and it is separated if j is finite.
nodes.by: Keel and Shigefumi Mori, 1997
nodes.note: It implies that a separated algebraic stack has a coarse moduli space, a best possible approximation to the stack by a separated algebraic space. Kollár proved a slightly weaker version in 1997.

nodes.name: Lambda g conjecture
nodes.statement: Let a₁, …, aₙ be positive integers with a₁ + … + aₙ = 2g − 3 + n. Then the integral of ψ₁^a₁ ⋯ ψₙ^aₙ λ_g over the Deligne–Mumford compactification of the moduli space of genus g curves with n marked points equals the multinomial coefficient (2g + n − 3)! / (a₁! ⋯ aₙ!) times the integral of ψ₁^(2g−2) λ_g over the compactification with one marked point.
nodes.by: First found by Ezra Getzler and Rahul Pandharipande, 1998, as a consequence of the Virasoro conjecture; proved by Faber and Pandharipande, 2003
nodes.note: Here λ_g is the gth Chern class of the Hodge bundle and the ψᵢ are first Chern classes of the cotangent line bundles. Together with the value ((2^(2g−1) − 1)/2^(2g−1)) · |B_2g|/(2g)! of the one-point integral, where B_2g is a Bernoulli number, it computes all such integrals.

nodes.name: Mori–Nagata theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be a noetherian reduced commutative ring with total ring of fractions K. Then the integral closure of A in K is a direct product of r Krull domains, where r is the number of minimal prime ideals of A.
nodes.by: Mori, 1953, and Nagata, 1955
nodes.note: It is a partial generalization of the Krull–Akizuki theorem, which concerns a one-dimensional noetherian domain.

nodes.name: Narasimhan–Seshadri theorem
nodes.statement: A holomorphic vector bundle over a compact Riemann surface is stable if and only if it comes from an irreducible projective unitary representation of the fundamental group. For degree zero bundles, it is stable if and only if it comes from an irreducible unitary representation of the fundamental group.
nodes.by: M. S. Narasimhan and C. S. Seshadri, 1965; another proof by Donaldson, 1983
nodes.note: Donaldson's version says a degree zero holomorphic vector bundle over a Riemann surface is stable if and only if it admits a flat unitary connection compatible with its holomorphic structure.

nodes.name: O'Nan–Scott theorem
nodes.statement: A maximal subgroup of the symmetric group Sym(Ω), where |Ω| = n, is one of the following: the stabilizer S_k × S_(n−k) of a k-set (intransitive); the stabilizer S_a wr S_b of a partition into b parts of size a, with n = ab (imprimitive); or a primitive group of one of these types: AGL(d,p), S_l wr S_k (the stabilizer of a product structure Ω = Δ^k), a group of diagonal type, or an almost simple group.
nodes.by: Leonard Scott, 1979, in an appendix to a paper for the Santa Cruz Conference on Finite Groups (Michael O'Nan independently proved the same result); a corrected statement by Michael Aschbacher and Scott; a complete version with a self-contained proof by M.W. Liebeck, Cheryl Praeger and Jan Saxl
nodes.note: The classification of finite simple groups is what makes the theorem so useful. Its real power is in splitting the finite primitive groups into types.

nodes.name: Parshin's conjecture
nodes.statement: For any smooth projective variety X defined over a finite field, the higher algebraic K-groups vanish up to torsion: Kᵢ(X) ⊗ ℚ = 0 for all i > 0.
nodes.by: Named after Aleksei Nikolaevich Parshin and Alexander Beilinson
nodes.note: It is also called the Beilinson–Parshin conjecture. It holds when X has dimension 0, by Quillen's computation of the K-groups of finite fields, and when X has dimension 1, by work of Harder.

nodes.name: Schur product theorem
nodes.statement: The Hadamard product (the entrywise product) of two positive definite matrices of the same size is again a positive definite matrix.
nodes.by: Issai Schur, 1911
nodes.note: A converse holds: if M is a symmetric matrix and the Hadamard product of M with N is positive definite for every positive definite matrix N, then M itself is positive definite.

nodes.name: Lasker–Noether theorem
nodes.statement: In a Noetherian commutative ring, every ideal is an intersection of finitely many primary ideals (a primary decomposition). The decomposition can be taken irredundant, and then the set of prime radicals of its parts is determined by the ideal, and each part whose radical is a minimal element of that set is determined too.
nodes.by: Lasker, 1905, for polynomial rings and convergent power series rings; Noether, 1921, in full generality
nodes.note: It extends the fundamental theorem of arithmetic to all Noetherian rings. It does not hold in general for non-commutative Noetherian rings.

nodes.name: Brauer–Suzuki theorem
nodes.statement: If a finite group has a generalized quaternion Sylow 2-subgroup and no non-trivial normal subgroups of odd order, then the group has a center of order 2. In particular, such a group cannot be simple.
nodes.by: Brauer and Suzuki, 1959; Suzuki, 1962; Brauer, 1964
nodes.note: It is generalized by Glauberman's Z* theorem.

nodes.name: Newton's identities
nodes.statement: For n variables x₁, …, xₙ, let p_k = x₁^k + … + xₙ^k be the k-th power sum and e_k the k-th elementary symmetric polynomial, the sum of all products of k different variables (with e_k = 0 for k > n). Then for every k ≥ 1, p_k = (−1)^(k−1)·k·e_k + ∑ (−1)^(j−1) e_j p_(k−j), where the sum runs over j from 1 to min(n, k−1).
nodes.by: Albert Girard, 1629; found by Isaac Newton around 1666, apparently in ignorance of Girard's work
nodes.note: Evaluated at the roots of a monic polynomial, they express the sums of k-th powers of the roots in terms of the coefficients, without finding the roots. They are also known as the Girard–Newton formulae.

nodes.name: Sylvester's law of inertia
nodes.statement: If S is a real symmetric matrix and P is any invertible real matrix of the same size, then PSPᵀ has the same numbers of positive, negative and zero eigenvalues as S. Equivalently, when S is transformed in this way into a diagonal matrix with entries 0, +1 and −1, the number of entries of each kind does not depend on the matrix P used.
nodes.by: James Joseph Sylvester, 1852
nodes.note: It is useful when PSPᵀ is diagonal, since its inertia can be read from the signs of the diagonal entries.

nodes.name: Cayley's theorem
nodes.statement: Every group G is isomorphic to a subgroup of a symmetric group. More precisely, G is isomorphic to a subgroup of Sym(G), the group of permutations of the underlying set of G, via the map sending each g to left multiplication by g.
nodes.by: Arthur Cayley, 1854, whose paper showed the correspondence is one-to-one but not explicitly that it is a homomorphism; later published by Walther Dyck, 1882
nodes.note: It unifies abstract groups with permutation groups, since every abstract group acts as a group of permutations. For a finite group of order n it gives an embedding into the symmetric group Sₙ.

nodes.name: Rational root theorem
nodes.statement: Take a polynomial equation aₙxⁿ + aₙ₋₁xⁿ⁻¹ + ⋯ + a₀ = 0 with integer coefficients, where a₀ and aₙ are not zero. Every rational solution p/q written in lowest terms has p dividing the constant term a₀ and q dividing the leading coefficient aₙ.
nodes.note: It is a special case, for a single linear factor, of Gauss's lemma on the factorization of polynomials. It is used to find all rational roots of a polynomial by checking a finite list of candidate fractions.

nodes.name: Schanuel's lemma
nodes.statement: Let R be a ring with identity. If 0 → K → P → M → 0 and 0 → K' → P' → M → 0 are short exact sequences of R-modules and P and P' are projective, then K ⊕ P' is isomorphic to K' ⊕ P.
nodes.by: Stephen Schanuel, 1958
nodes.note: It allows one to compare how far modules depart from being projective. It is used to define the Heller operator in the stable category and to describe dimension shifting.

nodes.name: Schur's lemma
nodes.statement: Let M and N be finite-dimensional irreducible representations of a group G, and let φ be a linear map from M to N that commutes with the action of the group. Then φ is either invertible or zero; and if M = N over an algebraically closed field such as ℂ, φ is a scalar multiple of the identity, so every element of the center of G acts on M as a scalar.
nodes.by: Named after Issai Schur, who used it to prove the Schur orthogonality relations; generalisations to Lie groups and Lie algebras are due to Jacques Dixmier and Daniel Quillen
nodes.note: Schur used it to develop the basics of the representation theory of finite groups. In the language of modules it says that the endomorphism ring of a simple module is a division ring.

nodes.name: Whitehead's lemma
nodes.statement: Let u be an invertible element of a ring. The 2×2 diagonal matrix with diagonal entries u and u⁻¹ equals the product e₂₁(u⁻¹) e₁₂(1−u) e₂₁(−1) e₁₂(1−u⁻¹), where eᵢⱼ(s) has 1s on the diagonal and s in position (i, j), so it can be reduced to the identity matrix by elementary transformations.
nodes.note: The name also refers to the result that the derived group of the stable general linear group over any ring is generated by elementary matrices, E(A) = [GL(A), GL(A)]. This fails in general for matrices of a fixed finite size, even over a field.

nodes.name: Closed-subgroup theorem
nodes.statement: If H is a closed subgroup of a Lie group G, then H is an embedded Lie group, with a smooth structure (and hence group topology) agreeing with the embedding.
nodes.by: Élie Cartan, 1930; a special case for groups of linear transformations was proved by John von Neumann, 1929
nodes.note: It is sometimes called Cartan's theorem. Conversely, an embedded Lie subgroup is closed, so a subgroup is an embedded Lie subgroup exactly when it is closed.

nodes.name: Milnor–Moore theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be a connected, graded, cocommutative Hopf algebra over a field of characteristic zero, where connected means A₀ is the field and A_n = 0 for negative n, and each graded piece A_n is finite-dimensional. Then the natural Hopf algebra homomorphism to A from the universal enveloping algebra U(P(A)) of the graded Lie algebra P(A) of primitive elements of A is an isomorphism.
nodes.by: John Milnor and John Coleman Moore, 1965
nodes.note: In algebraic topology the name usually refers to a corollary: for a pointed, simply connected space X, U(π_*(ΩX) ⊗ ℚ) is isomorphic to H_*(ΩX; ℚ), where ΩX is the loop space of X.

nodes.name: Posner's theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be a prime polynomial identity algebra with center Z. Then the ring A ⊗_Z Z₍₀₎ is a central simple algebra over Z₍₀₎, the field of fractions of Z.
nodes.by: Named after Ed Posner

nodes.name: Gelfand–Raikov theorem
nodes.statement: The points of a locally compact group G are separated by its irreducible unitary representations. For any two distinct elements g and h of G there is a Hilbert space H and an irreducible unitary representation ρ: G → U(H) with ρ(g) ≠ ρ(h).
nodes.by: Named after Gel'fand and Raikov; first published in 1943
nodes.note: It follows that a locally compact group is completely determined by its unitary representations.

nodes.name: Popescu's theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be a Noetherian ring and B a Noetherian algebra over it. Then the structure map A → B is a regular homomorphism if and only if B is a direct limit of smooth A-algebras.
nodes.by: Introduced by Dorin Popescu; another proof by Tetsushi Ogoma; proved by an alternate method and somewhat strengthened by Mark Spivakovsky
nodes.note: The usual proof of the Artin approximation theorem relies crucially on this theorem.

nodes.name: Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch theorem
nodes.statement: Let X and Y be smooth quasi-projective schemes over a field, let f: X → Y be a proper morphism, and let F be a bounded complex of coherent sheaves on X. Then ch(f_!F)·td(Y) = f_*(ch(F)·td(X)) in the Chow groups with rational coefficients, where f_! is the alternating sum of the higher direct images, f_* is the pushforward of cycles, ch is the Chern character and td is the Todd genus of the tangent bundle.
nodes.by: Alexander Grothendieck, first proof in a 1957 manuscript; written up and published by Armand Borel and Jean-Pierre Serre, 1958
nodes.note: It generalises the Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch theorem, which is essentially the special case where Y is a point and the field is the complex numbers. It turns the Riemann–Roch theorem from a statement about a single variety into one about a morphism between two varieties.

nodes.name: Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
nodes.statement: For any two vectors u and v in an inner product space, the absolute value of their inner product is at most the product of their norms: |⟨u, v⟩| ≤ ‖u‖ ‖v‖. The two sides are equal if and only if u and v are linearly dependent.
nodes.by: Cauchy (1821) for sums; Bunyakovsky (1859) and Schwarz (1888) for integrals
nodes.note: It covers finite sums, infinite series and integrals, depending on the inner product used. The triangle inequality in any inner product space follows from it.

nodes.name: Wigner–Eckart theorem
nodes.statement: Given a spherical tensor operator T of rank k and angular momentum states with quantum numbers j and j', there is a constant, the reduced matrix element, that does not depend on m, m' or q. For all m, m' and q, the matrix element ⟨j m|T_q|j' m'⟩ equals the Clebsch–Gordan coefficient ⟨j' m' k q|j m⟩ for coupling j' with k to get j, times this constant.
nodes.by: Eugene Wigner and Carl Eckart, who developed the formalism
nodes.note: It reduces many matrix elements to a single one: in the 4d → 2p example, one of 45 integrals determines the other 44.

nodes.name: Artin–Tate lemma
nodes.statement: Let A be a commutative Noetherian ring and B ⊆ C commutative algebras over A. If C is of finite type over A (a finitely generated algebra) and C is finite over B (a finitely generated module), then B is of finite type over A.
nodes.by: Emil Artin and John Tate, 1951
nodes.note: It was introduced to give a proof of Hilbert's Nullstellensatz. It is similar to the Eakin–Nagata theorem.

nodes.name: Bernstein–Kushnirenko theorem
nodes.statement: Take n finite subsets A₁, …, Aₙ of ℤⁿ and choose, for each i, a generic Laurent polynomial fᵢ in n variables whose exponents lie in Aᵢ. Then the system f₁ = … = fₙ = 0 has exactly n! V(Δ₁, …, Δₙ) solutions with all coordinates nonzero complex numbers, where V is the Minkowski mixed volume and Δᵢ is the convex hull of Aᵢ; if all the Aᵢ equal A, this number is n! times the volume of the convex hull of A.
nodes.by: Proved by David Bernstein and a coauthor, 1975; Askold Khovanskii found about 15 different proofs
nodes.note: It is also called the Bernstein–Khovanskii–Kushnirenko (BKK) theorem. Bézout's theorem gives another upper bound on the number of common zeros of n polynomials in n unknowns.

nodes.name: Gudkov's conjecture
nodes.statement: For an M-curve of even degree 2d, the number p of positive ovals and the number n of negative ovals satisfy p − n ≡ d² (mod 8), that is, p − n − d² is divisible by 8. Here an M-curve is a smooth real algebraic curve whose genus is k − 1, where k is the number of maximal components of the curve.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Dmitry Gudkov; proved by the combined works of Vladimir Arnold and Vladimir Rokhlin

nodes.name: Burnside's theorem
nodes.statement: If G is a finite group of order p^a q^b, where p and q are prime numbers and a and b are non-negative integers, then G is solvable.
nodes.by: Burnside, 1904
nodes.note: Hence each non-Abelian finite simple group has order divisible by at least three distinct primes. Burnside's proof used the representation theory of finite groups.

nodes.name: Cramer's theorem on algebraic curves
nodes.statement: In non-degenerate cases, n(n+3)/2 points in the real plane lying on an algebraic curve of degree n determine that curve uniquely. For example, a line is determined by 2 points, and a non-degenerate conic by 5 points in general position.
nodes.by: Gabriel Cramer, 1750
nodes.note: The number n(n+3)/2 is the number of coefficients left in a degree n polynomial equation in two variables once one coefficient is fixed at 1.

nodes.name: Ado's theorem
nodes.statement: Every finite-dimensional Lie algebra L over a field K of characteristic zero has a faithful linear representation on a finite-dimensional vector space V over K. So L is isomorphic to a subalgebra of the endomorphisms of V, that is, a Lie algebra of square matrices under the commutator bracket.
nodes.by: Igor Dmitrievich Ado, 1935
nodes.note: The restriction on the characteristic was later removed by Kenkichi Iwasawa.

nodes.name: Laplace expansion
nodes.statement: For an n × n matrix B and any row i, det(B) = ∑ⱼ (−1)^(i+j) bᵢⱼ mᵢⱼ, summed over j from 1 to n. Here bᵢⱼ is the entry in row i and column j, and mᵢⱼ is the determinant of the submatrix obtained by removing row i and column j. The same holds along any column j, summing over i.
nodes.by: Named after Pierre-Simon Laplace
nodes.note: It allows recursion on the size of matrices in proofs. For large matrices it is inefficient to compute compared with Gaussian elimination.

nodes.name: Rouché–Capelli theorem
nodes.statement: A system of linear equations in n variables with coefficients in a field K has a solution if and only if its coefficient matrix A and its augmented matrix have the same rank. If solutions exist, they form an affine subspace of Kⁿ of dimension n − rank(A).
nodes.note: It determines the number of solutions of a linear system from the ranks of its matrices. If K is a finite field, the number of solutions is |K|^(n − rank(A)).

nodes.name: Primitive element theorem
nodes.statement: Every separable field extension of finite degree is simple, that is, generated by a single element.
nodes.by: Proved in its modern form by Ernst Steinitz, 1910; Évariste Galois sketched a proof for a splitting field of a polynomial over the rationals in his First Memoir of 1831, published in 1846
nodes.note: It applies to all algebraic number fields, since every finite extension of the rational numbers is separable.

nodes.name: Lie's theorem
nodes.statement: Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, let π be a finite-dimensional representation of a solvable Lie algebra on a vector space V. Then there is a flag V = V₀ ⊃ V₁ ⊃ … ⊃ Vₙ = 0 of subspaces invariant under π, with codimension of Vᵢ equal to i. Equivalently, V has a basis in which all the transformations π(X) are upper triangular matrices.
nodes.note: It generalizes the result of Frobenius that commuting matrices are simultaneously upper triangularizable. A consequence is that a finite-dimensional solvable Lie algebra over a field of characteristic 0 has a nilpotent derived algebra.

nodes.name: Impossibility of doubling the cube
nodes.statement: Given the edge of a cube, it is impossible to construct, with only a compass and straightedge, the edge of a cube with twice the volume. Equivalently, the cube root of 2 is not a constructible number.
nodes.by: Pierre Wantzel, 1837
nodes.note: Every constructible number generates a field extension whose degree is a power of 2, while the cube root of 2 generates one of degree 3. The cube can be doubled by other means, such as conic sections, a marked ruler or origami.

nodes.name: Bauer–Fike theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be a diagonalizable n×n matrix with complex entries, written as A = VΛV⁻¹ with V an invertible matrix of eigenvectors and Λ diagonal, and let κₚ(V) = ‖V‖ₚ·‖V⁻¹‖ₚ be the condition number of V in the p-norm. Then for every eigenvalue μ of a perturbed matrix A + δA there is an eigenvalue λ of A with |λ − μ| ≤ κₚ(V)·‖δA‖ₚ.
nodes.by: Friedrich L. Bauer and C. T. Fike, 1960
nodes.note: The sensitivity of the eigenvalues is bounded by the condition number of the eigenvector matrix. For a normal matrix this number is 1 in the 2-norm, so every perturbed eigenvalue lies within ‖δA‖₂ of an eigenvalue of A.

nodes.name: Krull–Schmidt theorem
nodes.statement: If a group G satisfies both the ascending and the descending chain condition on normal subgroups, then any two ways of writing G as a direct product of finitely many indecomposable subgroups agree, and such a way exists. Precisely, if G = G₁ × … × G_k and G = H₁ × … × Hₗ are two such products, then k = l and, after reindexing the Hᵢ, each Gᵢ is isomorphic to Hᵢ and G = G₁ × … × Gᵣ × Hᵣ₊₁ × … × Hₗ for each r.
nodes.by: First proved by Joseph Wedderburn, 1909, for finite groups; Robert Remak, 1911; simplified by Otto Schmidt, 1913; extended by Wolfgang Krull, 1925, to abelian operator groups with ascending and descending chain conditions
nodes.note: A version for modules holds for modules of finite length. It fails in general for modules that are only Noetherian or only Artinian.

nodes.name: Schur–Zassenhaus theorem
nodes.statement: If G is a finite group and N is a normal subgroup whose order is coprime to the order of the quotient group G/N, then G is a semidirect product of N and G/N; equivalently, N has a complement in G. If moreover N or G/N is solvable, then all complements of N in G are conjugate.
nodes.by: Introduced by Zassenhaus, who credits the existence of a complement to Issai Schur
nodes.note: The solvability assumption always holds, but all known proofs of this use the much harder Feit–Thompson theorem. Without the coprime condition the theorem fails, as the cyclic group C₄ with its subgroup C₂ shows.

nodes.name: Cohn's irreducibility criterion
nodes.statement: Let b ≥ 2 be a natural number and let p(x) = aₖxᵏ + … + a₁x + a₀ be a polynomial whose coefficients all satisfy 0 ≤ aᵢ ≤ b−1. If p(b) is a prime number, then p(x) cannot be factored into polynomials of lower degree with integer coefficients (it is irreducible in ℤ[x]).
