In base 10, this means that if the decimal digits of a prime are used as the coefficients of a polynomial, that polynomial is irreducible.
nodes.by: The base 10 version is attributed to Arthur Cohn by Pólya and Szegő; the generalization to any base b is due to Brillhart, Filaseta and Odlyzko
nodes.note: Filaseta and Gross extended the base 10 case to coefficients up to a sharp bound of 49598666989151226098104244512918. The converse is the Bunyakovsky conjecture, which remains open.

nodes.name: Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt theorem
nodes.statement: Let L be a Lie algebra over a field K, let X be a totally ordered basis of L, and let h be the canonical K-linear map from L into the universal enveloping algebra U(L). Then the products h(x₁)·h(x₂)···h(xₙ) with x₁ ≤ x₂ ≤ … ≤ xₙ in X are distinct for distinct sequences, and together with the unit 1 they form a basis of U(L) as a K-vector space.
nodes.by: Alfredo Capelli proved the case of the general linear Lie algebra in four papers from the 1880s; Henri Poincaré stated it more generally in 1900; Garrett Birkhoff and Ernst Witt gave complete proofs in 1937
nodes.note: It gives an explicit description of the universal enveloping algebra of a Lie algebra. A corollary is that the canonical map L → U(L) is injective, so every Lie algebra over a field is isomorphic to a Lie subalgebra of an associative algebra.

nodes.name: Sherman–Morrison formula
nodes.statement: Let A be an invertible n×n real matrix and u, v column vectors in ℝⁿ. Then A + uvᵀ is invertible if and only if 1 + vᵀA⁻¹u ≠ 0, and in that case (A + uvᵀ)⁻¹ = A⁻¹ − (A⁻¹uvᵀA⁻¹) / (1 + vᵀA⁻¹u).
nodes.by: Named after Jack Sherman and Winifred J. Morrison; it appeared already in earlier publications, and the general form given here was published by Bartlett
nodes.note: It cheaply computes the inverse of a rank-1 update to a matrix whose inverse is already known. It is a special case of the Woodbury formula.

nodes.name: Steinitz exchange lemma
nodes.statement: Let U and W be finite subsets of a vector space V, where U is linearly independent and W spans V. Then U has at most as many elements as W, and there is a subset W′ of W with |W| − |U| elements such that U ∪ W′ spans V.
nodes.by: Named after Ernst Steinitz; Saunders Mac Lane generalized it to matroids
nodes.note: It can be used to show that any two bases of a finite-dimensional vector space have the same number of elements.

nodes.name: Jordan–Schur theorem
nodes.statement: There is a function f(n) such that every finite subgroup G of GL(n, ℂ), the group of invertible n-by-n complex matrices, has a subgroup H that is abelian and normal in G, with index (G : H) ≤ f(n).
nodes.by: Camille Jordan; Schur proved a more general result for periodic groups
nodes.note: Schur showed that the result also holds when G is only periodic, and better bounds for f(n) were found by Schur, Speiser, Blichfeldt and Collins. Collins and, separately, Larsen and Pink extended the theorem to finite subgroups of general linear groups over arbitrary fields.

nodes.name: Goursat's lemma
nodes.statement: Let G and G' be groups, and let H be a subgroup of G×G' whose projections onto G and onto G' are both surjective. Let N be the kernel of the projection to G' and N' the kernel of the projection to G. Then N can be viewed as a normal subgroup of G and N' as a normal subgroup of G', and the image of H in G/N × G'/N' is the graph of an isomorphism G/N ≅ G'/N'. This gives a one-to-one correspondence between subgroups of G×G' that project onto both factors and triples (N, N', f), where N is normal in G, N' is normal in G' and f is an isomorphism from G/N onto G'/N'.
nodes.by: Named after Édouard Goursat
nodes.note: It can be stated more generally in a Goursat variety, and in that form it implies the snake lemma.

nodes.name: Krull's theorem
nodes.statement: Every nonzero ring with a multiplicative identity 1 has at least one maximal ideal.
nodes.by: Wolfgang Krull, 1929, using transfinite induction
nodes.note: It has a simple proof using Zorn's lemma and is equivalent to Zorn's lemma, which is equivalent to the axiom of choice. For pseudo-rings, which lack an identity, it holds only for regular ideals.

nodes.name: Liouville's theorem on elementary antiderivatives
nodes.statement: Let F be a differential field and G an elementary extension of F (built from F by finitely many algebraic, logarithmic or exponential steps) that has the same constants as F. If some g in G satisfies Dg = f for an element f of F, then f = c₁·Df₁/f₁ + … + cₙ·Dfₙ/fₙ + Ds for some constants c₁, …, cₙ of F and some elements f₁, …, fₙ, s of F, so that an elementary antiderivative of f is an element of F plus constant multiples of logarithms of elements of F.
nodes.by: Joseph Liouville, 1833 to 1841
nodes.note: Some elementary functions, such as e^(−x²), have no elementary antiderivative. The theorem is a precursor to the Risch algorithm, which relies on it to find any elementary antiderivative.

nodes.name: Andrews–Curtis conjecture
nodes.statement: Every balanced presentation of the trivial group (one with the same number of generators and relations) can be transformed into a trivial presentation by a sequence of Nielsen transformations on the relators together with conjugations of relators.
nodes.by: James J. Andrews and Morton L. Curtis, 1965
nodes.note: It is widely believed to be false, but no counterexample is known. The Zeeman conjecture on collapsibility implies it.

nodes.name: Hilbert's seventeenth problem
nodes.statement: Every polynomial in any number of variables with real coefficients that takes only non-negative values at real points can be written as a sum of squares of rational functions (quotients of polynomials).
nodes.by: Posed by David Hilbert, 1900; solved in the affirmative by Emil Artin, 1927
nodes.note: Not every non-negative polynomial is a sum of squares of polynomials, which is why rational functions are allowed. Pfister showed that a positive semidefinite form in n variables is a sum of 2ⁿ squares, and Dubois showed that the answer is negative for general ordered fields.

nodes.name: Gordan's lemma
nodes.statement: Let A be a matrix of integers and let M be the set of non-negative integer solutions x of A·x = 0. Then there is a finite subset of M such that every element of M is a combination of the vectors in that subset with non-negative integer coefficients.
nodes.by: Named after Paul Gordan (1837–1912)
nodes.note: It can also be stated as: the semigroup of integral points in a rational convex polyhedral cone is finitely generated.

nodes.name: Sumihiro's theorem
nodes.statement: A normal algebraic variety with an action of a torus can be covered by torus-invariant affine open subsets.
nodes.by: Sumihiro, 1974
nodes.note: Neither the normality hypothesis nor the hypothesis that the acting group is a torus can be relaxed.

nodes.name: Serre's theorem on affineness
nodes.statement: Let X be a scheme with structure sheaf O_X. If X is quasi-compact and H¹(X, I) = 0 for every quasi-coherent ideal sheaf I of O_X-modules, then X is affine.
nodes.by: Jean-Pierre Serre, first published 1957
nodes.note: It gives sufficient conditions for a scheme to be affine, stated in terms of sheaf cohomology.

nodes.name: Kodaira vanishing theorem
nodes.statement: Let M be a compact Kähler manifold of complex dimension n, L a positive holomorphic line bundle on M, and K_M the canonical line bundle. Then the sheaf cohomology group H^q(M, K_M ⊗ L) is zero for every q > 0.
nodes.by: Kunihiko Kodaira
nodes.note: For q = 0, the dimension of the space of global sections then equals a holomorphic Euler characteristic, which can be computed with the Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch theorem.

nodes.name: Poincaré separation theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be an n × n real symmetric matrix and B an n × r matrix with BᵀB = I_r. Let λ₁ ≥ … ≥ λₙ be the eigenvalues of A and μ₁ ≥ … ≥ μ_r the eigenvalues of BᵀAB. Then λᵢ ≥ μᵢ ≥ λ_{n−r+i} for i = 1, …, r.
nodes.by: Named after Henri Poincaré
nodes.note: It is also known as the Cauchy interlacing theorem. BᵀAB can be seen as the orthogonal projection of A onto the subspace spanned by the columns of B.

nodes.name: Castelnuovo's contraction theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a smooth projective surface over ℂ and C a (−1)-curve on X, that is, a smooth rational curve of self-intersection number −1. Then there is a morphism from X to another smooth projective surface Y that contracts C to one point P and is an isomorphism outside C, so that X∖C is isomorphic to Y∖P.
nodes.by: Named after Guido Castelnuovo
nodes.note: It is used to construct the minimal model of a given smooth algebraic surface. The contraction is also called a blowdown, the inverse of a blowup.

nodes.name: Thompson replacement theorem
nodes.statement: Let P be a finite p-group for a prime p, let 𝒜 be the set of abelian subgroups of P of maximal order, and let B be an abelian subgroup of P. If A in 𝒜 normalizes B but is not normalized by B, then there is another A* in 𝒜 such that A* ∩ B is strictly larger than A ∩ B and [A*, A] normalizes A.
nodes.note: The Glauberman replacement theorem, introduced by Glauberman in 1968, generalizes it for odd p by weakening the condition that B is abelian.

nodes.name: Carlitz–Wan conjecture
nodes.statement: Let F_q be a finite field with q elements and d a positive integer. If gcd(d, q − 1) > 1, there are no exceptional polynomials of degree d over F_q.
nodes.by: The special case with q odd and d even was proposed by Leonard Carlitz, 1966, and proved by Fried, Guralnick, and Saxl, 1993. The general form was proposed by Daqing Wan, 1993, and proved by Hendrik Lenstra, 1995.
nodes.note: For q > d⁴, a polynomial is exceptional if and only if it is a permutation polynomial over F_q.

nodes.name: Decomposition theorem of Beilinson, Bernstein and Deligne
nodes.statement: For a proper map f: X → Y between algebraic varieties, the direct image Rf_*IC_X of the intersection cohomology complex of X is isomorphic to the direct sum ⊕ᵢ ᵖHⁱ(Rf_*IC_X)[−i] of its shifted perverse cohomology sheaves. Each summand is a semisimple perverse sheaf, that is, a direct sum of push-forwards of intersection cohomology sheaves.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Gelfand and MacPherson; first proved by Beilinson, Bernstein, Deligne and Gabber
nodes.note: It generalizes the decomposition for smooth proper maps that follows from the hard Lefschetz theorem. Other proofs were given by Saito using mixed Hodge modules and by de Cataldo and Migliorini using semismall maps.

nodes.name: Frobenius's theorem (group theory)
nodes.statement: If n divides the order of a finite group G, then the number of solutions of xⁿ = 1 in G is a multiple of n.
nodes.by: Frobenius, 1903
nodes.note: A more general version says that if C is a conjugacy class with h elements of a finite group G with g elements, then the number of elements k with kⁿ in C is a multiple of the greatest common divisor (hn, g).

nodes.name: Cartan–Dieudonné theorem
nodes.statement: Let V be an n-dimensional space with a non-degenerate symmetric bilinear form b, over a field whose characteristic is not 2. Then every orthogonal transformation of V is a composition of at most n reflections.
nodes.by: Named after Élie Cartan and Jean Dieudonné
nodes.note: In the Euclidean plane every orthogonal transformation is a reflection or a rotation, and a rotation is a composition of two reflections.

nodes.name: Artin–Zorn theorem
nodes.statement: Every finite alternative division ring is a finite field.
nodes.by: Max Zorn, 1930, who credited it to Emil Artin
nodes.note: It generalizes Wedderburn's little theorem, which says that finite associative division rings are fields. As a geometric consequence, every finite Moufang plane is the classical projective plane over a finite field.

nodes.name: Nine lemma
nodes.statement: In the category of groups or in any abelian category, take a commutative diagram with three rows and three columns of objects. If all columns and the two bottom rows are exact, the top row is exact; if all columns and the two top rows are exact, the bottom row is exact; if all columns and the top and bottom rows are exact and the map A₂ → C₂ across the middle row is the zero morphism, the middle row is exact; and the same three statements hold with rows and columns exchanged.
nodes.note: It can be proved by direct diagram chasing or by applying the snake lemma.

nodes.name: Adyan–Rabin theorem
nodes.statement: Let P be a Markov property of finitely presentable groups: P is preserved under isomorphism, some finitely presentable group has P, and some finitely presentable group cannot be embedded in any finitely presentable group with P. Then there is no algorithm that, given a finite presentation, decides whether the group it defines has property P.
nodes.by: Sergei Adyan, 1955, and independently Michael O. Rabin, 1958
nodes.note: It generalizes an earlier result for semigroups by Andrey Markov, Jr.

nodes.name: Brahmagupta–Fibonacci identity
nodes.statement: (a² + b²)(c² + d²) = (ac ± bd)² + (ad ∓ bc)², with either the upper or the lower signs taken together. So the product of two sums of two squares is a sum of two squares in two different ways. It holds for all integers, all rational numbers and in any commutative ring.
nodes.by: First proved by Diophantus of Alexandria; rediscovered and generalized by Brahmagupta; introduced in western Europe by Fibonacci, 1225
nodes.note: Brahmagupta proved the more general identity (a² + nb²)(c² + nd²) = (ac ± nbd)² + n(ad ∓ bc)². The identity is a special case of Euler's four-square identity and of Lagrange's identity.

nodes.name: McKay conjecture
nodes.statement: Let p be a prime, G a finite group and P a Sylow p-subgroup of G. The number of complex irreducible characters of G whose degree is not divisible by p equals the number of such characters of the normalizer N_G(P) of P in G.
nodes.by: John McKay stated a limited version (p = 2, simple groups) as a conjecture in 1971; first stated for arbitrary primes by Jon L. Alperin; a proof for all primes and all finite groups was announced by Britta Späth and Marc Cabanes, 2023
nodes.note: In 2007 Isaacs, Malle and Navarro reduced the conjecture to an inductive condition on finite simple groups. The case p = 2 was proven by Britta Späth and Gunter Malle in 2016.

nodes.name: Bass–Quillen conjecture
nodes.statement: For every regular Noetherian ring A, every rank r and every n, sending a module M to M ⊗ A[t₁, …, tₙ] gives a bijection between the isomorphism classes of rank r vector bundles (finitely generated projective modules) over A and those over the polynomial ring A[t₁, …, tₙ].
nodes.by: Hyman Bass and Daniel Quillen
nodes.note: When A is a field it says every projective module over a polynomial ring is free, which Quillen and Suslin proved (the Quillen–Suslin theorem). Lindel proved it in 1981 for A a smooth algebra over a field.

nodes.name: Ribet's lemma
nodes.statement: Let G₁×…×Gₙ be a product of perfect groups. Then any normal subgroup of this product that maps onto every factor Gᵢ, for i = 1, …, n, is the whole product group.
nodes.by: Introduced by Ribet, 1976
nodes.note: It gives conditions for a subgroup of a product of groups to be the whole product group.

nodes.name: Whitehead problem
nodes.statement: Every abelian group A with Ext¹(A, ℤ) = 0 is free. Here Ext¹(A, ℤ) = 0 means that every short exact sequence 0 → ℤ → B → A → 0 with B abelian splits.
nodes.by: Posed by J. H. C. Whitehead in the 1950s; Saharon Shelah proved it independent of ZFC
nodes.note: Shelah proved that the statement cannot be settled in ZFC: it holds if every set is constructible, and it fails if Martin's axiom and the negation of the continuum hypothesis hold. Stein proved it for countable groups.

nodes.name: Hanna Neumann conjecture
nodes.statement: If H and K are nontrivial finitely generated subgroups of a free group, then rank(H ∩ K) − 1 ≤ (rank(H) − 1)(rank(K) − 1). Here the rank of a group is the smallest size of a generating set.
nodes.by: Posed by Hanna Neumann, 1957; a strengthened version was proved independently by Joel Friedman and Igor Mineyev, 2011, and again by Andrei Jaikin-Zapirain, 2017
nodes.note: It was motivated by Howson's 1954 theorem that the intersection of two finitely generated subgroups of a free group is finitely generated.

nodes.name: Milnor conjecture (K-theory)
nodes.statement: For every field F of characteristic different from 2 and every n ≥ 0, the n-th Milnor K-group of F taken modulo 2, Kₙᴹ(F)/2, is isomorphic to the étale (Galois) cohomology group Hⁿ(F, ℤ/2ℤ).
nodes.by: Proposed by Milnor, 1970; proved by Vladimir Voevodsky
nodes.note: Its analogue for primes other than 2, the Bloch–Kato conjecture, was proved in 2009 through work of Voevodsky and Markus Rost and is now called the norm residue isomorphism theorem.

nodes.name: Skolem–Noether theorem
nodes.statement: Let A and B be simple rings with identity, let k be the center of B, and suppose B has finite dimension over k and A is a k-algebra. Then for any two k-algebra homomorphisms f, g: A → B there is a unit b in B with g(a) = b·f(a)·b⁻¹ for all a in A; in particular, every automorphism of a central simple k-algebra is inner.
nodes.by: Thoralf Skolem, 1927; later rediscovered by Emmy Noether
nodes.note: It is a fundamental result in the theory of central simple algebras.

nodes.name: Rank–nullity theorem
nodes.statement: For a linear transformation T between two vector spaces whose domain V is finite-dimensional, the dimension of V equals the rank of T (the dimension of its image) plus the nullity of T (the dimension of its kernel). Equivalently, for an m × n matrix, the rank plus the nullity equals n, the number of columns.
nodes.note: It follows that for linear transformations between vector spaces of equal finite dimension, either injectivity or surjectivity implies bijectivity.

nodes.name: Kempe's universality theorem
nodes.statement: Any bounded subset of an algebraic curve can be traced out by the motion of one of the joints in a suitably chosen linkage.
nodes.by: Alfred B. Kempe, 1876, whose proof was flawed; first complete proof, based on his ideas, 2002
nodes.note: Kempe saw that the linkages it gives would not be practical, because of their complexity.

nodes.name: Seesaw theorem
nodes.statement: Let L be a line bundle over X×T, where X is a complete variety and T is an algebraic set. Then the set of points t of T such that L is trivial on X×t is closed. If this set is the whole of T, then L is the pullback of a line bundle on T.
nodes.by: Introduced by André Weil in a course at the University of Chicago, 1954–1955; stated in terms of divisors by Lang, 1959
nodes.note: It is proved using proper base change and can be used to prove the theorem of the cube. Mumford gave a more precise version with a largest closed subscheme of T over which L is a pullback.

nodes.name: Lie product formula
nodes.statement: For arbitrary m × m real or complex matrices A and B, e^(A+B) is the limit as n → ∞ of (e^(A/n) e^(B/n))^n, where e^A is the matrix exponential. This holds even when A and B do not commute.
nodes.by: Named for Sophus Lie (1875); also called the Trotter product formula, after Hale Trotter
nodes.note: It replaces the exponential law e^(x+y) = e^x e^y for noncommuting matrices and is used to split a quantum evolution operator into alternating parts.

nodes.name: Yoneda lemma
nodes.statement: Let C be a locally small category, A an object of C, and F a functor from C to the category of sets. Then the natural transformations from the hom-functor Hom(A,−) to F are in one-to-one correspondence with the elements of the set F(A). A natural transformation Φ corresponds to the element u = Φ_A(id_A), and an element u corresponds to the natural transformation with Φ_X(f) = F(f)(u) for each morphism f: A → X.
nodes.by: Named after Nobuo Yoneda
nodes.note: It generalises Cayley's theorem from group theory and allows any locally small category to be embedded into a category of functors. The term "Yoneda lemma" was coined by Saunders Mac Lane, according to Yoshiki Kinoshita.

nodes.name: Cramer's rule
nodes.statement: Let A be an n × n matrix with nonzero determinant and b a column vector. Then the system Ax = b has a unique solution, given by xᵢ = det(Aᵢ) / det(A) for i = 1, …, n, where Aᵢ is A with its i-th column replaced by b.
nodes.by: Gabriel Cramer, who published the rule for an arbitrary number of unknowns in 1750; Colin Maclaurin published special cases in 1748
nodes.note: The rule holds for coefficients and unknowns in any field, not just the real numbers.

nodes.name: Prime avoidance lemma
nodes.statement: If an ideal I of a commutative ring R is contained in the union of finitely many prime ideals P₁, …, Pₙ, then I is contained in Pᵢ for some i.
nodes.note: A standard generalization allows I to be any additive subgroup of R that is closed under multiplication, and allows up to two of the ideals to be non-prime. When R contains an infinite field or a large enough finite field, the statement follows from the fact that a vector space over such a field is not a finite union of proper subspaces.

nodes.name: Fitting lemma
nodes.statement: Let M be a module over some ring. If M is indecomposable and has finite length, then every endomorphism of M is either an automorphism or nilpotent.
nodes.by: Named after Hans Fitting
nodes.note: It follows that the endomorphism ring of every finite-length indecomposable module is local. A version of it is often used in the representation theory of groups.

nodes.name: Schreier's lemma
nodes.statement: Let G be a group generated by a set S, H a subgroup of G, and R a set that contains the neutral element and exactly one element from each right coset Hg of H in G. Then H is generated by the elements rs·t⁻¹ with r in R and s in S, where t is the element of R that lies in the coset Hrs.
nodes.note: It implies that every subgroup of finite index in a finitely generated group is finitely generated. It is used in the Schreier–Sims algorithm and for finding a presentation of a subgroup.

nodes.name: AF+BG theorem
nodes.statement: Let F, G and H be homogeneous polynomials in three variables with complex coefficients, where H has higher degree than F and G, and F and G have no common factor other than a constant, so that their curves in the complex projective plane meet in finitely many points. If at every intersection point P the polynomial H lies in the ideal generated by F and G in the local ring at P, then H = AF + BG for homogeneous polynomials A and B of degrees deg H − deg F and deg H − deg G, where any two choices of A differ by a multiple of G and any two choices of B differ by a multiple of F.
nodes.by: Max Noether
nodes.note: It is also known as Max Noether's fundamental theorem. It generalizes Bézout's identity and refines Hilbert's Nullstellensatz for this case.

nodes.name: Erdős–Kaplansky theorem
nodes.statement: Let E be an infinite-dimensional vector space over a field K with a basis I. Then the dimension of the dual space E* equals the cardinality of K^I, the set of functions from I to K. This cardinal is strictly larger than the dimension of E, so E* is not isomorphic to E.
nodes.by: Named after Paul Erdős and Irving Kaplansky
nodes.note: More generally, for any infinite set I the dimension of the space of all functions from I to K equals the cardinality of K^I.

nodes.name: Engel's theorem
nodes.statement: A finite-dimensional Lie algebra 𝔤 is nilpotent if and only if, for every X in 𝔤, the adjoint map ad(X): Y ↦ [X, Y] is nilpotent, meaning ad(X)^k = 0 for some k.
nodes.by: Friedrich Engel sketched a proof in 1890; his student K.A. Umlauf gave a complete proof in 1891
nodes.note: It implies that a Lie algebra of matrices consisting of nilpotent matrices can be brought simultaneously to strictly upper triangular form.

nodes.name: Haboush's theorem
nodes.statement: Let G be a semisimple algebraic group over a field K, and let G act linearly on a K-vector space V. If v ≠ 0 in V is fixed by G, then there is a G-invariant polynomial F on V, without constant term, such that F(v) ≠ 0. The polynomial can be taken to be homogeneous, and if the characteristic is p > 0 its degree can be taken to be a power of p.
nodes.by: William Haboush proved Mumford's conjecture, about a decade after David Mumford posed the problem
nodes.note: In characteristic 0 this was well known, and F can even be taken to be linear. Haboush's theorem is often still called the Mumford conjecture.

nodes.name: Gromov's theorem on groups of polynomial growth
nodes.statement: A finitely generated group has polynomial growth if and only if it has a nilpotent subgroup of finite index.
nodes.by: Mikhail Gromov
nodes.note: Polynomial growth means the number of elements of length at most n, relative to a symmetric generating set, is bounded above by a polynomial in n.

nodes.name: Lie–Kolchin theorem
nodes.statement: Let G be a connected and solvable linear algebraic group defined over an algebraically closed field, and ρ: G → GL(V) a representation on a nonzero finite-dimensional vector space V. Then V has a 1-dimensional subspace L with ρ(G)(L) = L, equivalently a nonzero vector that is a common eigenvector of all ρ(g).
nodes.by: Kolchin, 1948; the analogous result for Lie algebras was proved by Lie, 1876
nodes.note: It follows that every irreducible finite-dimensional representation of such a group has dimension 1. The theorem can fail over a field that is not algebraically closed.

nodes.name: Lüroth's theorem
nodes.statement: Let K be a field and M a field between K and the rational function field K(X). Then there is a rational function f(X) in K(X) such that M = K(f(X)), so every intermediate field is a simple extension of K.
nodes.by: Jacob Lüroth, 1876

nodes.name: Correspondence theorem
nodes.statement: If N is a normal subgroup of a group G, then A ↦ A/N is a bijection from the set of all subgroups A of G containing N onto the set of all subgroups of the quotient group G/N. This bijection preserves inclusion, and A is a normal subgroup of G if and only if A/N is a normal subgroup of G/N.
nodes.note: Loosely, the subgroups of G/N have exactly the same structure as the subgroups of G containing N, with N collapsed to the identity element. It is also called the lattice theorem, and ambiguously the third or fourth isomorphism theorem.

nodes.name: Normal basis theorem
nodes.statement: Let K be a finite Galois extension of a field F with Galois group G. Then there is an element β in K such that the elements σ(β), for σ in G, form a basis of K as a vector space over F.
nodes.note: A basis of this kind is called a normal basis. The finer question of a normal integral basis belongs to Galois module theory in algebraic number theory.

nodes.name: Dimension theorem for vector spaces
nodes.statement: All bases of a vector space have equally many elements. This number, finite or infinite (a cardinal number), is the dimension of the vector space.
nodes.note: For finitely generated spaces the proof uses only elementary algebra and no form of the axiom of choice. In general the uniqueness of the cardinality of a basis requires only the ultrafilter lemma, which is strictly weaker than the axiom of choice.

nodes.name: Crystallographic restriction theorem
nodes.statement: Let G be a discrete group of isometries of two- or three-dimensional space (the orbit of every point is a set of isolated points) that includes translations spanning the whole space. Then every isometry in G of finite order has order 1, 2, 3, 4 or 6.
nodes.note: In particular the rotational symmetries of a lattice in 2 or 3 dimensions are restricted to 2-fold, 3-fold, 4-fold and 6-fold. In four or more dimensions more orders are possible; for example the hypercubic lattice has an eightfold rotational symmetry.

nodes.name: Krull's principal ideal theorem
nodes.statement: If R is a commutative Noetherian ring and I is a proper ideal of R generated by a single element, then every minimal prime ideal containing I has height at most one.
nodes.by: Named after Wolfgang Krull
nodes.note: It generalizes to Krull's height theorem: for a proper ideal generated by n elements, each minimal prime over it has height at most n. Both follow from the fundamental theorem of dimension theory in commutative algebra.

nodes.name: Shapley–Folkman lemma
nodes.statement: Let Q₁, …, Q_N be nonempty bounded subsets of D-dimensional real space ℝ^D, and let Q be their Minkowski sum (the set of all sums q₁ + … + q_N with each qₙ in Qₙ). Then every point of the convex hull of Q is a sum q₁ + … + q_N in which each qₙ lies in the convex hull of Qₙ, and for all but at most D of the indices n, qₙ lies in Qₙ itself.
nodes.by: Named after Lloyd Shapley and Jon Folkman; first published by the economist Ross M. Starr, 1969
nodes.note: It says that the Minkowski sum of many sets is approximately convex when the number of sets exceeds the dimension. It is used in economics, optimization and probability theory.

nodes.name: Pohlke's theorem
nodes.statement: Any three line segments in a plane that start at one point and do not lie on a single line can be seen as the parallel projection of three edges OU, OV, OW of a cube. Equivalently, any affine mapping of 3-dimensional space onto a plane is a composition of a similarity and a parallel projection.
nodes.by: Established by Karl Wilhelm Pohlke, 1853; first proof published by Hermann Amandus Schwarz, 1864
nodes.note: It is the fundamental theorem of axonometry.

nodes.name: Freshman's dream
nodes.statement: If p is a prime number and x and y are elements of a commutative ring of characteristic p, then (x + y)ᵖ = xᵖ + yᵖ. The same holds with the exponent p replaced by any power of p.
nodes.note: It means that raising to the power p is an endomorphism of the ring, the Frobenius endomorphism. For real numbers the equation (x + y)ⁿ = xⁿ + yⁿ is generally false.

nodes.name: Muller–Schupp theorem
nodes.statement: A finitely generated group has a context-free word problem, meaning that the words in its generators that equal the identity form a context-free language, if and only if the group is virtually free, meaning it has a free subgroup of finite index.
nodes.by: David Muller and Paul Schupp, 1983
nodes.note: The original 1983 formulation also required the group to be accessible, and Dunwoody's 1985 proof that finitely presented groups are accessible yields the modern form. It generalizes a 1971 theorem of Anisimov that the word problem is a regular language exactly when the group is finite.

nodes.name: Min-max theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be a compact self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space H, with positive eigenvalues λ₁ ≥ λ₂ ≥ … repeated according to multiplicity. Then each λ_k is the largest value, over all k-dimensional subspaces S of H, of the minimum of (Ax, x) over unit vectors x in S, and it is also the smallest value, over all (k − 1)-dimensional subspaces S, of the maximum of (Ax, x) over unit vectors x orthogonal to S.
nodes.note: It is also called the Courant–Fischer–Weyl min-max principle and is used to prove the Cauchy interlacing theorem. For a non-Hermitian matrix the Rayleigh quotient can exceed every eigenvalue.

nodes.name: Cayley–Bacharach theorem
nodes.statement: If two cubic curves in the projective plane meet in nine different points, then every cubic curve that passes through any eight of those points also passes through the ninth.
nodes.by: Arthur Cayley and Isaak Bacharach, generalizing to cubics a related result on conics first proved by Michel Chasles
nodes.note: Pascal's theorem and Pappus's hexagon theorem are special cases. It can also be used to prove that the group law on elliptic curves is associative.

nodes.name: Capelli's identity
nodes.statement: Let x_ij (i, j = 1, ..., n) be commuting variables and let E_ij = ∑ over a from 1 to n of x_ia ∂/∂x_ja. Then the column-determinant of the matrix with entries E_ij + (n−i)δ_ij, expanded keeping the factors in column order, equals the product det(x_ij) · det(∂/∂x_ij), as differential operators.
nodes.by: Named after Capelli, 1887
nodes.note: It is an analogue of det(AB) = det(A) det(B) for certain matrices with noncommuting entries. The only price for the noncommutativity is the small correction (n−i)δ_ij on the left-hand side.

nodes.name: Cauchy–Binet formula
nodes.statement: Let A be an m × n matrix and B an n × m matrix, with entries from any commutative ring. Then det(AB) equals the sum, over all subsets S of {1, …, n} of size m, of det(A_S) · det(B_S), where A_S is the m × m matrix of the columns of A with indices in S and B_S is the m × m matrix of the rows of B with indices in S.
nodes.by: Named after Augustin-Louis Cauchy and Jacques Philippe Marie Binet
nodes.note: It generalises the statement that the determinant of a product of square matrices is the product of their determinants. If n < m the sum is empty and det(AB) = 0.

nodes.name: Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch theorem
nodes.statement: Let E be a holomorphic vector bundle on a compact complex manifold X of complex dimension n. Then the holomorphic Euler characteristic χ(X, E) = ∑ (−1)^i dim H^i(X, E), the alternating sum over i = 0 to n of the dimensions of the sheaf cohomology groups, equals the integral over X of ch(E) td(X), where ch(E) is the Chern character of E and td(X) is the Todd class of the holomorphic tangent bundle of X.
nodes.by: Friedrich Hirzebruch, 1954
nodes.note: It generalizes the classical Riemann–Roch theorem on Riemann surfaces to complex algebraic varieties of higher dimensions. It paved the way for the Grothendieck–Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch theorem.

nodes.name: Abhyankar's conjecture
nodes.statement: Let p be a prime, K an algebraically closed field of characteristic p, C a nonsingular algebraic curve over K of genus g, and S a nonempty set of s + 1 points of C. A finite group G is the Galois group of a Galois extension of the function field K(C) that is ramified only over S if and only if G/p(G) can be generated by at most s + 2g elements, where p(G) is the subgroup generated by all Sylow p-subgroups of G.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Shreeram Abhyankar, 1957; soluble case solved by Serre, 1990; proved in 1994 by work of Michel Raynaud and David Harbater
nodes.note: It is a special type of inverse Galois problem. Raynaud proved the case where C is the projective line, and Harbater the general case.

nodes.name: Abhyankar's inequality
nodes.statement: For an extension K/k of valued fields, the transcendence degree of K/k is at least the transcendence degree of the residue field extension plus the rank of the quotient of the valuation groups, where the rank of an abelian group A is dim_ℚ(A ⊗ ℚ).
nodes.by: Abhyankar, 1956

nodes.name: Adjunction formula
nodes.statement: Let X be a smooth algebraic variety or smooth complex manifold and Y a smooth subvariety of X, with inclusion i and ideal sheaf I. Then the canonical bundle of Y satisfies ω_Y ≅ i*ω_X ⊗ det(I/I²)^∨, where ∨ denotes the dual line bundle; in particular, for a smooth divisor D on X, the canonical classes satisfy K_D = (K_X + D)|_D.
nodes.note: It relates the canonical bundle of a variety and a hypersurface inside it. The genus-degree formula for plane curves can be deduced from it.

nodes.name: Alperin–Brauer–Gorenstein theorem
nodes.statement: A finite simple group with quasidihedral or wreathed Sylow 2-subgroups is isomorphic either to a three-dimensional projective special linear group or projective special unitary group over a finite field of odd order, depending on a certain congruence, or to the Mathieu group M₁₁.
nodes.by: Alperin, Brauer and Gorenstein, 1970
nodes.note: The proof took 261 pages.

nodes.name: Amitsur–Levitzki theorem
nodes.statement: For any n × n matrices A₁, ..., A₂ₙ with entries in a commutative ring, the standard polynomial of degree 2n vanishes: the sum over all permutations σ of {1, ..., 2n} of sgn(σ) A_σ(1) ⋯ A_σ(2n) equals 0.
nodes.by: Shimshon Amitsur and Jacob Levitzki, 1950
nodes.note: In particular, matrix rings are polynomial identity rings such that the smallest identity they satisfy has degree exactly 2n.

nodes.name: Andreotti–Frankel theorem
nodes.statement: If V is a smooth complex affine variety of complex dimension n, or more generally any Stein manifold of complex dimension n, then V admits a Morse function with critical points of index at most n. Hence V is homotopy equivalent to a CW complex of real dimension at most n, and the integral homology and cohomology groups of V vanish in all degrees above n.
nodes.by: Aldo Andreotti and Theodore Frankel, 1959
nodes.note: In particular, every closed connected complex submanifold of ℂʳ of complex dimension n has the homotopy type of a CW complex of real dimension at most n.

nodes.name: Artin approximation theorem
nodes.statement: Let f(x, y) = 0 be a system of polynomial equations with coefficients in a field k, and let c be a positive integer. For every solution ŷ(x) made of formal power series over k, there is a solution y(x) made of algebraic power series that agrees with ŷ(x) modulo (x)^c, that is, in all terms of total degree below c.
nodes.by: Artin, 1969 (the algebraic version); an earlier version on complex analytic solutions was proved in 1968
nodes.note: It shows that formal power series with coefficients in a field k are well approximated by algebraic functions on k. It is used to deduce that certain formal moduli spaces of deformations exist as schemes.

nodes.name: Auslander–Buchsbaum formula
nodes.statement: If R is a commutative Noetherian local ring and M is a non-zero finitely generated R-module of finite projective dimension, then pd_R(M) + depth(M) = depth(R), where pd is the projective dimension.
nodes.by: Maurice Auslander and David Buchsbaum, 1957
nodes.note: It implies that a Noetherian local ring is regular if and only if it has finite global dimension.

nodes.name: Auslander–Buchsbaum theorem
nodes.statement: Every regular local ring is a unique factorization domain.
nodes.by: Auslander and Buchsbaum, 1959, who showed it for dimension 3; Nagata, 1958, had shown that the dimension 3 case implies the general case

nodes.name: Ax–Grothendieck theorem
nodes.statement: If P is a polynomial map from ℂⁿ to itself that is injective (it never sends two different points to the same point), then P is also surjective, so it is a bijection. More generally, an injective regular map from an algebraic variety over an algebraically closed field to itself is bijective.
nodes.by: James Ax and Alexander Grothendieck, independently
nodes.note: Grothendieck's proof first treats finite fields and their algebraic closures, then transfers the result to the complex numbers. The theorem can be used to prove the Garden of Eden theorem for cellular automata.

nodes.name: B-theorem
nodes.statement: If C is the centralizer of an involution of a finite group, then every component of C/O(C) is the image of a component of C.
nodes.note: It was formerly known as the B-conjecture.

nodes.name: Baer–Suzuki theorem
nodes.statement: Let C be a conjugacy class of a finite group. If any two elements of C generate a nilpotent subgroup, then all elements of C are contained in a nilpotent subgroup.
nodes.by: Baer, 1957, and Suzuki, 1965; Alperin and Lyons gave a short elementary proof in 1971

nodes.name: Bass conjecture
nodes.statement: For every finitely generated ℤ-algebra A that is a regular ring, the algebraic K-groups Kₙ(A) are finitely generated for all n ≥ 0. Equivalently, for every finitely generated ℤ-algebra A, the K-groups of its finitely generated modules (the G-theory of A) are finitely generated.
nodes.by: Hyman Bass
nodes.note: Daniel Quillen proved it for rings and schemes of dimension at most 1. Without regularity, ordinary K-groups can fail to be finitely generated: the ring ℤ[x, y]/x² has an infinitely generated K₁.

nodes.name: Beauville–Laszlo theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be a ring and f a non-zero divisor in A, with Â the completion of A at Af. Let F be an A_f-module and G an Â-module with no f-torsion, together with an isomorphism φ from G_f to F ⊗ Â. Then there is an A-module M with isomorphisms M_f ≅ F and M ⊗ Â ≅ G that are consistent with φ.
nodes.by: Arnaud Beauville and Yves Laszlo, 1995
nodes.note: It allows one to glue two sheaves over an infinitesimal neighborhood of a point on an algebraic curve.

nodes.name: Beck's monadicity theorem
nodes.statement: A functor U: C → D is monadic if and only if three conditions hold: U has a left adjoint; U reflects isomorphisms (if U(f) is an isomorphism then so is f); and C has coequalizers of U-split parallel pairs, and U preserves those coequalizers.
nodes.by: Beck, 1968
nodes.note: It is often stated in dual form for comonads. It is closely tied to descent theory, and most cases of faithfully flat descent are special cases of it.

nodes.name: Belyi's theorem
nodes.statement: Any non-singular algebraic curve defined by algebraic number coefficients represents a compact Riemann surface that is a ramified covering of the Riemann sphere, ramified at three points only.
nodes.by: G. V. Belyi, 1979
nodes.note: The result was considered surprising at the time. It spurred Grothendieck to develop his theory of dessins d'enfant.

nodes.name: Finsler's lemma
nodes.statement: Let Q and L be real symmetric n×n matrices. Then the following are equivalent: (1) xᵀQx < 0 for every nonzero x in ℝⁿ with xᵀLx = 0; (2) there is a real number μ such that Q − μL is negative definite.
nodes.by: Named after Paul Finsler
nodes.note: It is equivalent to other lemmas used in optimization and control theory, such as Yakubovich's S-lemma, and is widely used in robust optimization and with linear matrix inequalities.

nodes.name: Density theorem
nodes.statement: Every presheaf of sets on a category C is a colimit of representable presheaves in a canonical way. Precisely, a presheaf F is the colimit of the diagram formed by the category of elements of F, its forgetful functor to C, and the Yoneda embedding of C into the presheaves on C.
nodes.note: For simplicial sets, which are presheaves on the simplex category, it says each simplicial set is a colimit of standard simplices.

nodes.name: Frobenius reciprocity
nodes.statement: Let G be a finite group and H a subgroup of G. For any complex-valued class functions ψ on H and φ on G, ⟨Ind ψ, φ⟩_G = ⟨ψ, Res φ⟩_H, where Ind ψ is the class function on G induced from ψ, Res φ is the restriction of φ to H, and ⟨·,·⟩ is the standard inner product on class functions.
nodes.by: Named after Ferdinand Georg Frobenius
nodes.note: It was originally stated in terms of character theory. In the language of modules and categories, induction is left adjoint to restriction, and for finite groups each is both left and right adjoint to the other.

nodes.name: Solovay–Kitaev theorem
nodes.statement: Let G be a finite set of elements of SU(2) that contains its own inverses and generates a dense subgroup of SU(2). Then there is a constant c such that for any U in SU(2) and any ε > 0, some sequence S of gates from G of length O(log^c(1/ε)) satisfies ‖S − U‖ ≤ ε in operator norm, and such a sequence can be found efficiently. The same holds in SU(d) for any fixed d.
nodes.by: First announced by Robert M. Solovay in 1995; independently proven by Alexei Kitaev in 1997
nodes.note: A consequence is that a quantum circuit of m constant-qubit gates can be approximated to error ε by a circuit of O(m log^c(m/ε)) gates from a finite universal gate set.

nodes.name: Birkhoff–Grothendieck theorem
nodes.statement: Every holomorphic vector bundle on the complex projective line is holomorphically isomorphic to a direct sum of line bundles O(a₁) ⊕ … ⊕ O(aₙ). This representation is unique up to permuting the summands.
nodes.by: Proved by Grothendieck, 1957; more or less equivalent to Birkhoff factorization, introduced by Birkhoff in 1909
nodes.note: The same result holds for algebraic vector bundles over the projective line over any field. It gives a classification of all coherent sheaves on the complex projective line.

nodes.name: Blattner's conjecture
nodes.statement: Restrict a discrete series representation of a semisimple group G with infinitesimal character λ to a maximal compact subgroup K. Then the representation of K with highest weight μ occurs with multiplicity ∑ ε(w) Q(w(μ+ρ_c) − λ − ρ_n), summed over w in the Weyl group W_K of K. Here Q(v) is the number of ways v can be written as a sum of non-compact positive roots, ρ_c and ρ_n are half the sums of the compact and non-compact roots, and ε is the sign character of W_K.
nodes.by: Named after Robert James Blattner, who raised it as a question; first in print in Schmid, 1968; proved by Hecht and Schmid, 1975 (linear semisimple groups) and by Enright, 1979
nodes.note: Blattner's formula is what one gets by formally restricting the Harish-Chandra character formula for a discrete series representation to the maximal torus of a maximal compact group.

nodes.name: Bogomolov–Miyaoka–Yau inequality
nodes.statement: For a compact complex surface of general type with first and second Chern classes c₁ and c₂, the Chern numbers satisfy c₁² ≤ 3c₂. If equality holds, the surface is a quotient of a ball.
nodes.by: Proved independently by Yau and Miyaoka, 1977, after Van de Ven (1966) and Bogomolov (1978) proved weaker versions with the constant 3 replaced by 8 and 4
nodes.note: It restricts the possible topological types of the underlying real 4-manifold. The inequality is best possible and is false in positive characteristic.

nodes.name: Borel fixed-point theorem
nodes.statement: If G is a connected, solvable, linear algebraic group acting regularly on a non-empty, complete algebraic variety V over an algebraically closed field k, then V has a point fixed by G.
nodes.by: Borel, 1956
nodes.note: It generalizes the Lie–Kolchin theorem, which assumes that V is a projective variety.

nodes.name: Borel–Weil–Bott theorem
nodes.statement: Let G be a semisimple Lie group or algebraic group over ℂ, B a Borel subgroup, λ an integral weight and L_λ the associated line bundle on G/B. Write w*λ = w(λ+ρ) − ρ, where w is in the Weyl group and ρ is half the sum of the positive roots. If no w makes w*λ dominant, all cohomology groups H^i(G/B, L_λ) are zero. Otherwise there is a unique such w, H^i(G/B, L_λ) is zero for i ≠ ℓ(w), and H^ℓ(w)(G/B, L_λ) is the dual of the irreducible highest-weight representation of G with highest weight w*λ.
nodes.by: Borel–Weil theorem by Armand Borel and André Weil; extension to higher cohomology by Raoul Bott
nodes.note: The case where λ is dominant and w is the identity gives the classical Borel–Weil theorem.

nodes.name: Brauer's theorem on induced characters
nodes.statement: For a finite group G, the character ring of G is generated, as an abelian group, by characters induced from one-dimensional representations of elementary subgroups of G. A subgroup is elementary if it is a direct product of a cyclic group and a group whose order is a power of a prime.
nodes.by: Richard Brauer, 1946
nodes.note: It removes the factor |G| from Artin's induction theorem, at the cost of using more subgroups. J.A. Green showed in 1955 that no smaller collection than the Brauer elementary subgroups would work.

nodes.name: Brauer's theorem on forms
nodes.statement: Let K be a field such that for every r > 0 there is ψ(r) with the property that for n ≥ ψ(r) every equation a₁x₁^r + … + aₙxₙ^r = 0 with coefficients in K has a solution in K that is not all zero. Then for any positive integer degrees r₁,…,r_k and any l ≥ 0 there is a number ω(r₁,…,r_k,l) such that, for n ≥ ω, any homogeneous polynomials f₁,…,f_k in n variables over K of degrees r₁,…,r_k all vanish on some l-dimensional affine subspace M of Kⁿ.
nodes.by: Named after Richard Brauer
nodes.note: Applied to the p-adic numbers, it shows that a homogeneous equation of degree r over the p-adic numbers has a non-trivial solution if the number of variables is sufficiently large.

nodes.name: Brauer–Fowler theorem
nodes.statement: If a finite group G has even order g > 2, then it has a proper subgroup of order greater than g^(1/3).
nodes.by: Richard Brauer and K. A. Fowler
nodes.note: The proof counts involutions. The same count gives that only finitely many finite simple groups have a given centralizer of an involution, which motivated part of the classification of finite simple groups.

nodes.name: Cartan–Brauer–Hua theorem
nodes.statement: Let D be a division ring and K a division subring of D containing the identity of D. If xKx⁻¹ ⊆ K for every nonzero x in D, then either K is contained in the center of D or K = D.
nodes.by: Named after Richard Brauer, Élie Cartan, and Hua Luogeng
nodes.note: Equivalently, if the multiplicative group of K is a normal subgroup of the group of nonzero elements of D, then K is either central or equal to D.

nodes.name: Castelnuovo–de Franchis theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a projective, non-singular complex algebraic surface, and let ω₁ and ω₂ be two differentials of the first kind on X that are linearly independent but have wedge product 0. Then there is a non-singular algebraic curve C, a morphism φ: X → C, and differentials of the first kind ω₁′ and ω₂′ on C such that φ*(ω₁′) = ω₁ and φ*(ω₂′) = ω₂.
nodes.by: Guido Castelnuovo and Michele de Franchis
nodes.note: The converse, that two such pullbacks have wedge product 0, is immediate.

nodes.name: Chasles–Cayley–Brill formula
nodes.statement: A correspondence T of valence k from an algebraic curve C of genus g to itself has d + e + 2kg united points, where d and e are the degrees of T and of its inverse.
nodes.by: Michel Chasles introduced the formula for genus 0, Arthur Cayley stated the general formula without proof, and Alexander von Brill gave the first proof.
nodes.note: The number of united points is the intersection number of the correspondence with the diagonal of C×C.

nodes.name: Chevalley's structure theorem
nodes.statement: A smooth connected algebraic group over a perfect field has a unique normal smooth connected affine algebraic subgroup such that the quotient is an abelian variety.
nodes.by: Chevalley (1960, announced 1953), Barsotti, and Rosenlicht (1956)
nodes.note: A consequence is that any algebraic group over a field is quasi-projective. Over non-perfect fields there is still a smallest normal connected linear subgroup with abelian variety quotient, but it need not be smooth.

nodes.name: Chevalley–Iwahori–Nagata theorem
nodes.statement: Let a linear algebraic group G act linearly on a finite-dimensional vector space V. If the ring of invariant polynomials is finitely generated and all orbits of G on V are closed, then the map from V/G to the spectrum of the ring of invariant polynomials is an isomorphism.
nodes.by: Named after Claude Chevalley, Nagayoshi Iwahori and Masayoshi Nagata

nodes.name: Chevalley–Shephard–Todd theorem
nodes.statement: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field K and let G be a finite subgroup of GL(V) whose order is coprime to the characteristic of K. Call an element of GL(V) a pseudoreflection if it is not the identity and fixes a subspace of codimension 1. Then the following are equivalent: G is generated by pseudoreflections; the algebra of invariants K[V]^G is a polynomial algebra; K[V]^G is a regular ring; K[V] is a free module over K[V]^G; K[V] is a projective module over K[V]^G.
nodes.by: Shephard and Todd, 1954 (case-by-case proof for subgroups of the complex general linear group); uniform proof by Chevalley, 1955; extended to arbitrary fields in the non-modular case by Jean-Pierre Serre
nodes.note: Over the complex numbers, the first condition says that G is a complex reflection group. Shephard and Todd classified such groups.

nodes.name: Chow's moving lemma
nodes.statement: Given algebraic cycles Y and Z on a nonsingular quasi-projective variety X, there is another algebraic cycle Z' that is rationally equivalent to Z on X and such that Y and Z' intersect properly. Even if Z is effective, Z' cannot in general be chosen effective.
nodes.by: Chow, 1956
nodes.note: It is one of the key ingredients in developing intersection theory and the Chow ring, where it is used to show the uniqueness of the theory.

nodes.name: Chow's lemma
nodes.statement: If X is a scheme that is proper over a noetherian base S, then there is a projective S-scheme X′ and a surjective S-morphism f: X′ → X that restricts to an isomorphism f⁻¹(U) ≅ U for some dense open subset U of X.
nodes.by: Named after Wei-Liang Chow
nodes.note: Roughly, it says that a proper morphism is fairly close to being a projective morphism. If X and X′ are both irreducible, then f is a birational morphism.

nodes.name: Clifford's theorem on special divisors
nodes.statement: Let D be an effective special divisor on a Riemann surface C, meaning ℓ(K − D) > 0 for the canonical divisor K, and let d be its degree. Then 2(ℓ(D) − 1) ≤ d. Equality holds only if D is zero or a canonical divisor, or if C is a hyperelliptic curve and D is linearly equivalent to an integral multiple of a hyperelliptic divisor.
nodes.by: Clifford, 1878
nodes.note: It shows that the Clifford index of a curve is non-negative. The index measures how far the curve is from being hyperelliptic.

nodes.name: Cohen structure theorem
nodes.statement: A complete Noetherian local ring that contains a field is a quotient of a formal power series ring in finitely many variables over its residue field, by some ideal. A complete Noetherian local ring that does not contain a field is a quotient of a formal power series ring in finitely many variables over a Cohen ring with the same residue field.
nodes.by: Cohen, 1946
nodes.note: A Cohen ring is a field or a complete characteristic zero discrete valuation ring whose maximal ideal is generated by a prime number p. The theorem implies three conjectures of Krull.

nodes.name: Courant minimax principle
nodes.statement: Let A be a real symmetric n×n matrix with eigenvalues in decreasing order λ₁ ≥ λ₂ ≥ … ≥ λₙ. For each k, λₖ equals the minimum, over all (k−1)×n matrices C, of the largest value of ⟨Ax,x⟩ over unit vectors x (‖x‖ = 1) with Cx = 0.
nodes.by: Named after Richard Courant
nodes.note: It generalizes to eigenvalues of positive self-adjoint operators on Hilbert spaces, where it is commonly used to study the Sturm–Liouville problem.

nodes.name: De Franchis theorem
nodes.statement: For compact Riemann surfaces, or more generally algebraic curves, X and Y of genus g > 1, the set of non-constant morphisms from X to Y is finite.
nodes.by: Named after M. De Franchis (1875–1946)
nodes.note: A special case is that the automorphism group of such a curve is finite. Gerd Faltings used it in an important way to prove the Mordell conjecture.

nodes.name: Determinantal conjecture
nodes.statement: For any two n-by-n normal complex matrices A and B, the determinant of A + B lies in the convex hull of the n! points ∏ᵢ (λ(A)ᵢ + λ(B)_σ(i)), where λ(A)ᵢ and λ(B)ᵢ are the eigenvalues of A and B and σ runs over the symmetric group Sₙ.
nodes.by: Marcus (1972) and de Oliveira (1982)

nodes.name: ELSV formula
nodes.statement: Let g ≥ 0 and n ≥ 1 be integers and let k₁, …, kₙ be positive integers. Let h be the Hurwitz number counting connected genus g ramified coverings of the Riemann sphere with n numbered preimages of the point at infinity of multiplicities k₁, …, kₙ and m more simple branch points, where m = ∑kᵢ + n + 2g − 2 and a covering with automorphism group G is counted with weight 1/|G|. Then h equals m!/#Aut(k₁, …, kₙ) times the product of kᵢ^kᵢ/kᵢ! times the integral over the moduli space of stable curves of genus g with n marked points of c(E*)/((1 − k₁ψ₁)⋯(1 − kₙψₙ)), where E is the Hodge bundle and ψᵢ is the first Chern class of the cotangent line bundle at the i-th marked point.
nodes.by: Announced by Ekedahl, Lando, Shapiro and Vainshtein, 1999, with an erroneous sign; proved in full generality by Graber and Vakil, 2003
nodes.note: Several fundamental results in the intersection theory of moduli spaces of curves can be deduced from it, including the Witten conjecture and the Virasoro constraints.

nodes.name: Eilenberg–Ganea theorem
nodes.statement: Let G be a finitely presented group and n ≥ 3 an integer. If the cohomological dimension of G with integer coefficients is at most n, then there is an n-dimensional aspherical CW complex X whose fundamental group is G.
nodes.by: Named after Samuel Eilenberg and Tudor Ganea; first published 1957
nodes.note: Its converse also holds: if X is an aspherical n-dimensional CW complex with fundamental group G, then the cohomological dimension of G is at most n. The case n = 2 is the open Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture.

nodes.name: Enriques–Babbage theorem
nodes.statement: Every canonical curve is a set-theoretic intersection of quadrics, or is trigonal, or is a plane quintic.
nodes.by: Enriques, 1919, and Babbage, 1939

nodes.name: Leibniz formula for determinants
nodes.statement: For an n×n matrix A with entries a(i,j) from a field, det(A) is the sum over all permutations τ of {1, …, n} of sgn(τ)·a(1,τ(1))·a(2,τ(2))···a(n,τ(n)), where sgn(τ) is +1 for an even permutation and −1 for an odd one.
nodes.by: Named after Gottfried Leibniz
nodes.note: Evaluating the formula directly takes on the order of n!·n operations, so in practice the determinant is computed by LU decomposition in O(n³) operations.

nodes.name: Farrell–Jones conjecture
nodes.statement: For a group G and a ring R, the map from E_VCYC(G), the classifying space of G for its virtually cyclic subgroups, to a point induces an isomorphism from the equivariant K-homology KR^G_*(E_VCYC(G)) to KR^G_*(point), which is the algebraic K-theory K_*(R[G]) of the group ring. The L-theoretic version, with L-theory in place of K-theory, is analogous.
nodes.by: Named after F. Thomas Farrell and Lowell E. Jones
nodes.note: If it is true, computations of K-theory and L-theory of group rings can be reduced to virtually cyclic subgroups. It is known for hyperbolic, CAT(0) and solvable groups among others, and no counterexamples are known.

nodes.name: Fitting's theorem
nodes.statement: If M and N are nilpotent normal subgroups of a group G, then their product MN is also a nilpotent normal subgroup of G. If M is nilpotent of class m and N is nilpotent of class n, then MN is nilpotent of class at most m + n.
nodes.by: Hans Fitting
nodes.note: It follows that the subgroup generated by finitely many nilpotent normal subgroups is nilpotent, which is used to show that the Fitting subgroup of a finite group is nilpotent. For infinitely many such subgroups this can fail.

nodes.name: Focal subgroup theorem
nodes.statement: Let G be a finite group with Sylow p-subgroup P. Then P ∩ [G,G] equals P ∩ ker(v), where v is the transfer homomorphism from G to P/[P,P], and both equal the subgroup generated by all x⁻¹y with x and y in P and x conjugate to y in G.
nodes.by: Higman, 1953
nodes.note: It relates transfer and fusion of elements in a Sylow subgroup. These ideas are applied to local criteria for p-nilpotence and to showing that a finite group has a normal subgroup of index p.

nodes.name: Frobenius determinant theorem
nodes.statement: Take the multiplication table of a finite group G and replace each entry g with a variable x_g. Over the complex numbers, the determinant of this table factors into r different irreducible polynomials, no two of which are multiples of each other, where r is the number of conjugacy classes of G, and each factor appears raised to a power equal to its own degree.
nodes.by: First stated as a conjecture by Richard Dedekind in a letter of 1896 to F. G. Frobenius, who proved it
nodes.note: Frobenius proved it by methods which began the representation theory of finite groups.

nodes.name: Fröberg conjecture
nodes.statement: For generic homogeneous polynomials g₁, …, g_k in ℂ[x₁, …, x_n] of degrees a₁, …, a_k, the Hilbert series of ℂ[x₁, …, x_n]/⟨g₁, …, g_k⟩ is (1+t+t²+⋯)ⁿ (1−t^a₁)⋯(1−t^a_k), truncated at its first negative term.
nodes.by: Fröberg, 1985; generalized by Iarrobino, 1997 (the Fröberg–Iarrobino conjecture)
nodes.note: It concerns the possible Hilbert functions of a set of forms.

nodes.name: Fulton–Hansen connectedness theorem
nodes.statement: Let V and W be irreducible algebraic subvarieties of a projective space P over an algebraically closed field. If dim(V) + dim(W) > dim(P), then the intersection of V and W is connected.
nodes.by: William Fulton and Johan Hansen, 1979
nodes.note: A more general form says that for a morphism f from a projective variety Z to Pⁿ × Pⁿ with dim f(Z) > n, the preimage of the diagonal is connected.

nodes.name: Fundamental theorem of cyclic groups
nodes.statement: Every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic. For a finite cyclic group of order n, the order of every subgroup divides n, and there is exactly one subgroup for each divisor of n.

nodes.name: Gabriel's theorem
nodes.statement: A connected quiver has only finitely many isomorphism classes of indecomposable representations (it is of finite type) if and only if its underlying graph, ignoring the directions of the arrows, is one of the ADE Dynkin diagrams A_n, D_n, E₆, E₇, E₈. The indecomposable representations then correspond one to one with the positive roots of the root system of that diagram, and the coefficients of a positive root in terms of the simple roots give the dimensions of the indecomposable's vector spaces at the vertices.
nodes.by: Pierre Gabriel, 1972

nodes.name: Gabriel–Popescu theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be a Grothendieck category, G a generator of A, and R the ring of endomorphisms of G. Then the functor S from A to the category of right R-modules, defined by S(X) = Hom(G,X), is full and faithful and has an exact left adjoint. It follows that A is equivalent to the Serre quotient of the category of right R-modules by a certain localizing subcategory.
nodes.by: Nicolae Popescu and Pierre Gabriel, 1964
nodes.note: It characterizes Grothendieck categories as quotients of module categories. The embedding S is left-exact but not necessarily right-exact.

nodes.name: Genus–degree formula
nodes.statement: An irreducible plane curve of degree d in the projective plane has arithmetic genus g = ½(d−1)(d−2). If the curve is non-singular, its geometric genus equals g. If its only singularities are ordinary ones, its geometric genus is smaller than g by ½r(r−1) for each ordinary singularity of multiplicity r.
nodes.note: It can be proved from the adjunction formula. For elliptic curves, which are cubics, it gives genus 1.

nodes.name: Gerbaldi's theorem
nodes.statement: There exist six ternary quadratic forms (quadratic forms in three variables) that are nondegenerate, linearly independent and pairwise apolar.
nodes.by: Gerbaldi, 1882
nodes.note: These six forms are permuted by the Valentiner group.

nodes.name: Giambelli's formula
nodes.statement: For a partition λ = (λ₁, …, λ_r), the Schubert class σ_λ equals the determinant of the r × r matrix whose entry in row i and column j is the special Schubert class σ_{λᵢ+j−i}.
nodes.by: Named after Giovanni Giambelli
nodes.note: It may be derived as a consequence of Pieri's formula. The same identity for Schur functions is the first Jacobi-Trudi identity.

nodes.name: Gabriel–Rosenberg reconstruction theorem
nodes.statement: A quasi-separated scheme can be recovered from the category of quasi-coherent sheaves on it.
nodes.by: Pierre Gabriel, 1962; named after Pierre Gabriel and Alexander L. Rosenberg
nodes.note: The theorem is taken as a starting point for noncommutative algebraic geometry.

nodes.name: Jouanolou's trick
nodes.statement: If X is a scheme quasi-projective over an affine scheme, then there exist a vector bundle E over X and an E-torsor W over X such that W is affine. In particular W comes with a surjective map to X and is Zariski-locally on X an affine space bundle.
nodes.by: Jean-Pierre Jouanolou; generalized by Robert Thomason
nodes.note: The variety W is homotopy-equivalent to X and is affine, which is technically advantageous. Thomason obtained the same conclusion for quasicompact and quasiseparated schemes with an ample family of line bundles.

nodes.name: Kleiman's theorem
nodes.statement: Let a connected algebraic group G act transitively on an algebraic variety X over an algebraically closed field k, and let V₁ → X and V₂ → X be morphisms of varieties. Then G contains a nonempty open subset such that for each g in it, gV₁ ×_X V₂ is either empty or of pure dimension dim V₁ + dim V₂ − dim X, and, if in addition the Vᵢ are smooth and k has characteristic zero, gV₁ ×_X V₂ is smooth (the Kleiman–Bertini theorem).
nodes.by: Kleiman, 1974
nodes.note: The dimension statement is a version of Chow's moving lemma: after perturbing cycles on X, their intersection has the expected dimension.

nodes.name: Matsusaka's big theorem
nodes.statement: Given an ample line bundle L on a compact complex manifold X, there is an integer m, depending only on the Hilbert polynomial of L, such that the tensor power Lⁿ is very ample for all n ≥ m.
nodes.by: Teruhisa Matsusaka, 1972; named by Lieberman and Mumford, 1975
nodes.note: The theorem has an application to the theory of Hilbert schemes.

nodes.name: Multi-homogeneous Bézout theorem
nodes.statement: Split the variables into k groups, the i-th with nᵢ + 1 variables for positive integers n₁, …, nₖ, let n = n₁ + … + nₖ, and record the multi-degree of a polynomial that is homogeneous of degree aᵢ in the i-th group as the linear form a₁t₁ + … + aₖtₖ. Then the common complex zeros of n such polynomials with multi-degrees d₁, …, dₙ, not counting zeros where all variables of some group vanish, either form a set of positive dimension or consist of B points counted with multiplicities, where B is the coefficient of t₁^n₁ ⋯ tₖ^nₖ in the product d₁ ⋯ dₙ.
nodes.by: Igor Shafarevich
nodes.note: It generalizes Bézout's theorem, which counts the isolated common zeros of homogeneous polynomials, and often gives a much smaller bound when there are infinitely many solutions at infinity.

nodes.name: Zariski's finiteness theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be a normal domain that is finitely generated as an algebra over a field k. If L is a subfield of the field of fractions of A that contains k and has transcendence degree at most 2 over k, then the k-subalgebra L ∩ A is finitely generated.
nodes.note: As a special case it gives a positive answer to Hilbert's 14th problem for the polynomial ring in two variables.

nodes.name: Abundance conjecture
nodes.statement: For every projective variety X with Kawamata log terminal singularities over a field k, if the canonical bundle K_X is nef, then K_X is semi-ample, that is, mK_X is base-point free for some m > 0.
nodes.note: Important cases have been proven by Caucher Birkar.

nodes.name: Glennie's identity
nodes.statement: In a special Jordan algebra with product •, define the triple product {X,Y,Z} = X•(Y•Z) − Y•(Z•X) + Z•(X•Y). Then for all X, Y, Z in the algebra, 2{{Z,{X,Y,X},Z}, Y, Z•X} − {Z,{X,{Y,X•Z,Y},X},Z} = 2{X•Z, Y, {X,{Z,Y,Z},X}} − {X,{Z,{Y,X•Z,Y},Z},X}.
nodes.by: Charles M. Glennie, 1963
nodes.note: Glennie used it to establish s-identities that hold in special Jordan algebras but not in all Jordan algebras. It first appeared in his 1963 Yale PhD thesis.

nodes.name: Goddard–Thorn theorem
nodes.statement: Let V be a representation of the Virasoro algebra with a non-degenerate bilinear form for which each Lᵢ is adjoint to L₋ᵢ, on which the central element c acts as 24, which is the direct sum of finite-dimensional L₀-eigenspaces Vⁱ with integer eigenvalues i ≥ 0, and on which a group G acts preserving this grading. Let P¹_r be the degree r part (r in the two-dimensional even unimodular Lorentzian lattice II₁,₁) of the space of vectors v in V ⊗ V_{II₁,₁}, the tensor product with the lattice vertex algebra of II₁,₁, with L₀v = v and Lₙv = 0 for all n > 0. Then P¹_r modulo the nullspace of its bilinear form is naturally isomorphic, as a G-module with invariant bilinear form, to V^{1−(r,r)/2} if r ≠ 0 and to V¹ ⊕ ℝ² if r = 0.
nodes.by: Conjectured in another form by Lovelace, 1971; named after Peter Goddard and Charles Thorn; statement in the form given by Borcherds, 1992
nodes.note: Also called the no-ghost theorem, because in the original statement the induced inner product is positive definite, so there are no vectors of negative norm. Borcherds used it in his proof of the monstrous moonshine conjecture.

nodes.name: Goldie's theorem
nodes.statement: A ring is semiprime and right Goldie (of finite uniform dimension as a right module over itself, with the ascending chain condition on right annihilators of subsets) if and only if it has a semisimple Artinian right classical ring of quotients.
nodes.by: Alfred Goldie, 1950s
nodes.note: It applies to semiprime right Noetherian rings. The structure of the ring of quotients is then determined by the Artin–Wedderburn theorem.

nodes.name: Goncharov conjecture
nodes.statement: For a field F, Goncharov's complex Γ_F(n), placed in degrees 1 to n and running from B_n(F) through B_{n−1}(F) ⊗ F^×_ℚ down to Λⁿ F^×_ℚ, has i-th cohomology isomorphic to the motivic cohomology group H^i_mot(F, ℚ(n)).
nodes.by: Goncharov
nodes.note: The conjecture suggests that the cohomology of certain motivic complexes coincides with pieces of K-groups. It extends a conjecture due to Zagier.

nodes.name: Gorenstein–Walter theorem
nodes.statement: Let G be a finite group with a dihedral Sylow 2-subgroup, and let O(G) be its maximal normal subgroup of odd order. Then G/O(G) is isomorphic to a 2-group, or to the alternating group A₇, or to a subgroup of PΓL₂(q) containing PSL₂(q), for q an odd prime power.
nodes.by: Gorenstein and Walter

nodes.name: Grothendieck's connectedness theorem
nodes.statement: If A is a complete Noetherian local ring whose spectrum is k-connected and f is in the maximal ideal of A, then Spec(A/fA) is (k − 1)-connected. Here a Noetherian scheme is k-connected if its dimension is greater than k and the complement of every closed subset of dimension less than k is connected.
nodes.note: It is a local analogue of Bertini's theorem.

nodes.name: Grothendieck trace formula
nodes.statement: Let k be a finite field, l a prime invertible in k, X a smooth k-scheme of dimension n and 𝓕 a constructible ℚ_l-sheaf on X. Then for every finite field extension E of k, the sum over all points x of X(E) of the trace of Frobenius F_E on the stalk 𝓕_x equals ∑ from i = 0 to 2n of (−1)ⁱ times the trace of F_E on the compactly supported l-adic cohomology Hⁱ_c(X over the algebraic closure of k, 𝓕); for the constant sheaf ℚ_l the left side is the number of E-points of X.
nodes.note: It is an analogue of the Lefschetz fixed-point theorem. Using it to express the zeta function of a variety over a finite field through traces of Frobenius on cohomology is one of the steps in the proof of the Weil conjectures.

nodes.name: Theorem of the highest weight
nodes.statement: For a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra 𝔤, every finite-dimensional irreducible representation has a unique highest weight, which is dominant integral; two such representations with the same highest weight are isomorphic; and every dominant integral element is the highest weight of one, so highest weights match these representations one to one with the dominant integral elements. For a connected compact Lie group K the same holds with integral replaced by analytically integral, and the two notions coincide when K is simply connected.
nodes.by: Élie Cartan, 1913; the compact Lie group version is due to Hermann Weyl
nodes.note: It is one of the key pieces of the representation theory of semisimple Lie algebras. The hardest part is constructing an irreducible representation with a prescribed highest weight.

nodes.name: Hahn embedding theorem
nodes.statement: Every linearly ordered abelian group G can be embedded as an ordered subgroup of the additive group ℝ^Ω with the lexicographical order. Here Ω is the set of Archimedean equivalence classes of G, and ℝ^Ω is the set of all functions from Ω to ℝ that vanish outside a well-ordered set.
nodes.by: Named after Hans Hahn; Gravett (1956) gives a clear statement and proof, and the papers of Clifford (1954) and Hausner and Wendel (1952) together give another proof
nodes.note: When G is Archimedean, the theorem reduces to Hölder's theorem: a linearly ordered abelian group is Archimedean if and only if it is a subgroup of the ordered additive group of the real numbers.

nodes.name: Hall–Higman theorem
nodes.statement: Let G be a p-solvable group with no normal p-subgroup other than the trivial one, acting faithfully on a vector space over a field of characteristic p, and let x in G have order pⁿ, so that its minimal polynomial is (X − 1)^r for some r ≤ pⁿ. Then r = pⁿ; or p is a Fermat prime, the Sylow 2-subgroups of G are non-abelian and r ≥ pⁿ − pⁿ⁻¹; or p = 2, the Sylow q-subgroups of G are non-abelian for some Mersenne prime q = 2^m − 1 less than 2ⁿ, and r ≥ 2ⁿ − 2ⁿ⁻ᵐ.
nodes.by: Hall and Graham Higman, 1956
nodes.note: It describes the possible minimal polynomials of an element of prime power order in a representation of a p-solvable group.

nodes.name: Haran's diamond theorem
nodes.statement: Let K be a Hilbertian field and L a separable extension of K. If there are two Galois extensions N and M of K such that L is contained in the compositum NM but in neither N nor M, then L is Hilbertian.
nodes.by: Haran; the name was coined by Jarden
nodes.note: It gives a general sufficient condition for a separable extension of a Hilbertian field to be Hilbertian, and implies Weissauer's theorem.

nodes.name: Harish-Chandra's regularity theorem
nodes.statement: Every invariant eigendistribution on a semisimple Lie group or Lie algebra is given by a locally integrable function. Here invariant means invariant under conjugation by the group, and eigendistribution means an eigenvector of the center of the universal enveloping algebra.
nodes.by: Harish-Chandra, 1963
nodes.note: In particular, every character of an irreducible unitary representation on a Hilbert space is a locally integrable function. Harish-Chandra also proved a similar theorem for semisimple p-adic groups.

nodes.name: Harnack's curve theorem
nodes.statement: For a real algebraic curve of degree m in the real projective plane, the number c of connected components satisfies (1 − (−1)^m)/2 ≤ c ≤ (m−1)(m−2)/2 + 1. Every number of components in this range can be attained.
nodes.by: Named after Axel Harnack
nodes.note: The maximum is one more than the maximum genus of a curve of degree m and is attained only by nonsingular curves. The theorem formed the background to Hilbert's sixteenth problem.

nodes.name: Haynsworth inertia additivity formula
nodes.statement: Let H be a Hermitian matrix partitioned into blocks H₁₁, H₁₂, H₁₂*, H₂₂ with H₁₁ nonsingular, and let the inertia In of a Hermitian matrix be the triple (number of positive, number of negative, number of zero eigenvalues). Then In(H) = In(H₁₁) + In(H/H₁₁), where H/H₁₁ = H₂₂ − H₁₂* H₁₁⁻¹ H₁₂ is the Schur complement of H₁₁ in H.
nodes.by: Emilie Virginia Haynsworth
nodes.note: If H₁₁ is singular the formula does not hold. A 1974 generalization by Carlson, Haynsworth and Markham gives inequalities for the numbers of positive and negative eigenvalues.

nodes.name: Hermite's law of reciprocity
nodes.statement: The degree m covariants of a binary form of degree n correspond to the degree n covariants of a binary form of degree m. Equivalently, the representations S^m S^n ℂ² and S^n S^m ℂ² of GL₂ are isomorphic.
nodes.by: Hermite, 1854

nodes.name: Fundamental lemma (Langlands program)
nodes.statement: Let F be a local field, G an unramified group over F (a quasi-split reductive group that splits over an unramified extension of F), and H an unramified endoscopic group of G associated to a character κ. If γ_H and γ_G represent stable conjugacy classes in H and G, with the class of γ_G the transfer of the class of γ_H, then SO_γ_H(1_K_H) = Δ(γ_H, γ_G)·O^κ_γ_G(1_K_G): the stable orbital integral on H of the characteristic function of a hyperspecial maximal compact subgroup K_H equals the transfer factor Δ times the κ-orbital integral on G of the characteristic function of a hyperspecial maximal compact subgroup K_G.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Langlands, 1983; proved by Gérard Laumon and Ngô Bảo Châu for unitary groups, then by Ngô, 2010, for general reductive groups, building on reductions by Jean-Loup Waldspurger
nodes.note: It relates orbital integrals on a reductive group to stable orbital integrals on its endoscopic groups, as needed for Langlands' strategy based on the Arthur–Selberg trace formula. Ngô was awarded the Fields Medal in 2010 for the proof.

nodes.name: Hilbert–Burch theorem
nodes.statement: Let R be a local ring with an ideal I, and suppose 0 → Rᵐ → Rⁿ → R → R/I → 0 is a free resolution of the R-module R/I. Then m = n − 1, and I = aJ where a is a regular element of R and J is a depth-2 ideal, namely the first Fitting ideal of I, generated by the determinants of the minors of size m of the matrix of the map Rᵐ → Rⁿ.
nodes.by: David Hilbert, 1890, for polynomial rings; a more general version by Burch
nodes.note: It describes the structure of some free resolutions of a quotient of a local or graded ring when the quotient has projective dimension 2.

nodes.name: Hochster–Roberts theorem
nodes.statement: Rings of invariants of linearly reductive groups acting on regular rings are Cohen–Macaulay. In other words, if V is a rational representation of a linearly reductive group G over a field k, then there are algebraically independent invariant homogeneous polynomials f₁, …, f_d such that k[V]^G is a free finite graded module over k[f₁, …, f_d].
nodes.by: Melvin Hochster and Joel L. Roberts, 1974
nodes.note: In characteristic 0 it also follows from Boutot's 1987 result on rational singularities. In characteristic p > 0 there are reductive, even finite, groups acting on polynomial rings whose rings of invariants are not Cohen–Macaulay.

nodes.name: Hodge index theorem
nodes.statement: Let V be a non-singular projective surface over an algebraically closed field and H the class of a hyperplane section. In the space D of rational divisor classes on V up to algebraic equivalence, the subspace spanned by H has a complementary subspace on which the intersection pairing is negative definite. So the signature of the intersection pairing is (1, ρ(V) − 1), where ρ(V) is the finite dimension of D.
nodes.by: W. V. D. Hodge, in the 1930s, for varieties over the complex numbers; it had been a conjecture of the Italian school of algebraic geometry
nodes.note: Hodge proved it over the complex numbers, and it holds over general algebraically closed fields. ρ(V) is the rank of the Néron–Severi group.

nodes.name: Farkas' lemma
nodes.statement: Let A be a real m × n matrix and b a vector in ℝᵐ. Then exactly one of the following holds: the system Ax = b has a solution x whose entries are all nonnegative, or there is a vector y in ℝᵐ such that every entry of Aᵀy is nonnegative and bᵀy < 0.
nodes.by: Gyula Farkas; the formulation given is due to Gale, Kuhn and Tucker (1951)
nodes.note: Geometrically, a vector either lies in the cone spanned by the columns of A or is separated from it by a hyperplane. It is the key result underpinning linear programming duality.

nodes.name: Fischer's inequality
nodes.statement: Let M be a positive-semidefinite (p+q)×(p+q) complex matrix written in blocks with rows (A, B) and (B*, C), where A is p×p and C is q×q. Then det(M) ≤ det(A)·det(C), and if M is positive-definite, equality holds exactly when every entry of B is 0.
