nodes.note: Applied to 1×1 blocks it gives Hadamard's inequality as a corollary. Conversely, Fischer's inequality can be proved from Hadamard's inequality.

nodes.name: Weibel's conjecture
nodes.statement: For a Noetherian scheme X of finite Krull dimension d, the K-groups K_i(X) vanish for all i < −d. Moreover, K_i(X) = K_i(X × 𝔸^r) for all i ≤ −d and every r.
nodes.by: Proposed by Weibel, 1980; proven in full generality by Kerz, Strunk and Tamme, 2018
nodes.note: It gives a criterion for the vanishing of negative algebraic K-theory groups. Kelly, Saito and Tamme generalized it in 2024 to quasi-compact quasi-separated derived schemes, using the valuative dimension.

nodes.name: Isomorphism extension theorem
nodes.statement: Let F be a field, E an algebraic extension field of F, and φ an isomorphism from F onto a field F'. Then φ can be extended to an isomorphism τ from E onto an algebraic extension E' of F', which is a subfield of the algebraic closure of F'.
nodes.note: For field extensions of infinite degree the proof depends on Zorn's lemma.

nodes.name: Jordan's theorem on primitive permutation groups
nodes.statement: Let G be a primitive permutation group that is a subgroup of the symmetric group S_n. If G contains a p-cycle for some prime number p < n − 2, then G is either the whole symmetric group S_n or the alternating group A_n.
nodes.by: Camille Jordan
nodes.note: A p-cycle moves exactly p points, so the condition p < n − 2 means the cycle has at least three fixed points. The statement can be generalized to the case that p is a prime power.

nodes.name: Jørgensen's inequality
nodes.statement: If A and B generate a non-elementary discrete subgroup of SL₂(ℂ), then |Tr(A)² − 4| + |Tr(ABA⁻¹B⁻¹) − 2| ≥ 1.
nodes.by: Jørgensen, 1976
nodes.note: It gives a quantitative estimate of the discreteness of the group. It is used to prove the existence of cusp neighborhoods in hyperbolic 3-manifolds.

nodes.name: Kalman–Yakubovich–Popov lemma
nodes.statement: Let A, B and M be real matrices of sizes n×n, n×m and (n+m)×(n+m), with M symmetric, det(jωI − A) ≠ 0 for every real ω, and (A, B) controllable; then [(jωI − A)⁻¹B; I]* M [(jωI − A)⁻¹B; I] ≤ 0 for every ω in ℝ ∪ {∞} if and only if there is a real symmetric n×n matrix P with M + [[AᵀP + PA, PB], [BᵀP, 0]] ≤ 0. With both inequalities strict, the equivalence holds even when (A, B) is not controllable.
nodes.by: First formulated and proved by Vladimir Andreevich Yakubovich, 1962 (strict inequality); nonstrict case published by Rudolf E. Kálmán, 1963; restriction on control dimension removed by Gantmakher and Yakubovich and independently by Vasile Mihai Popov, 1964
nodes.note: The lemma can be seen as a generalization of the Lyapunov equation in stability theory. It relates a linear matrix inequality to a condition in the frequency domain.

nodes.name: Kawamata–Viehweg vanishing theorem
nodes.statement: If L is a big nef line bundle (for example, an ample line bundle) on a complex projective manifold with canonical line bundle K, then the coherent cohomology groups H^i(L⊗K) vanish for all positive i.
nodes.by: Proved independently by Viehweg and Kawamata, 1982
nodes.note: It extends the Kodaira vanishing theorem to logarithmic pairs.

nodes.name: Kempf vanishing theorem
nodes.statement: Let G be a reductive algebraic group over an algebraically closed field, B a Borel subgroup, and L(λ) the line bundle associated to λ. If λ is a dominant weight of B, then the higher cohomology groups H^i(G/B, L(λ)) vanish for all i > 0.
nodes.by: Kempf, 1976; simpler proofs by Andersen and Haboush, 1980
nodes.note: In characteristic 0 it is a special case of the Borel–Weil–Bott theorem, but unlike that theorem it still holds in positive characteristic.

nodes.name: Kodaira embedding theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a compact Kähler manifold and L a holomorphic line bundle on X. Then L is a positive line bundle if and only if there is a holomorphic embedding of X into some complex projective space ℙᴺ such that the pullback of 𝒪(1) equals the m-th tensor power of L for some m > 0.
nodes.by: Kunihiko Kodaira
nodes.note: It says which compact Kähler manifolds are non-singular projective varieties over the complex numbers, that is, which complex manifolds are defined by homogeneous polynomials.

nodes.name: Kurosh subgroup theorem
nodes.statement: Let G = A∗B be a free product of groups and H a subgroup of G. Then H is the free product of a free group F(X), freely generated by a subset X of G, with subgroups g_i A_i g_i⁻¹ and f_j B_j f_j⁻¹, where each A_i is a subgroup of A, each B_j is a subgroup of B, and the g_i, f_j are elements of G. The same holds for free products with arbitrarily many factors.
nodes.by: Alexander Kurosh, 1934
nodes.note: In modern terms it is a corollary of the basic results of Bass–Serre theory about groups acting on trees.

nodes.name: L-balance theorem
nodes.statement: If X is a finite group and T is a 2-subgroup of X, then the 2-layer of the centralizer of T in X is contained in the 2-layer of X. Here the 2-layer of a group is the product of all its 2-components, the minimal subnormal subgroups mapping onto components of X/O(X).
nodes.by: Gorenstein and Walter, 1975
nodes.note: A consequence is that for commuting involutions a and b of a group G, L₂′(L₂′(C_a) ∩ C_b) = L₂′(L₂′(C_b) ∩ C_a), which is the property called L-balance.

nodes.name: Lange's conjecture
nodes.statement: Let C be a smooth projective curve of genus at least 2. For generic vector bundles E₁ and E₂ on C of ranks and degrees (r₁, d₁) and (r₂, d₂), a generic extension 0 → E₁ → E → E₂ → 0 has E stable, provided that the slope d₁/r₁ is less than the slope d₂/r₂.
nodes.by: Formulated by Lange; proved by Montserrat Teixidor i Bigas and Barbara Russo, 1999
nodes.note: Generic here means a generic point in the moduli space of semistable vector bundles on C, and for the extension a generic point of Ext¹(E₂, E₁).

nodes.name: Lang's theorem
nodes.statement: If G is a connected smooth algebraic group over a finite field F_q and σ: G → G, x ↦ x^q is the Frobenius, then the morphism of varieties G → G, x ↦ x⁻¹σ(x) is surjective.
nodes.by: Introduced by Serge Lang
nodes.note: It implies that H¹(F_q, G) vanishes, so every G-bundle on Spec F_q is trivial. It also plays a basic role in the theory of finite groups of Lie type.

nodes.name: Sims conjecture
nodes.statement: There is an integer-valued function f such that for every primitive permutation group G on a finite set S, every point α of S and every orbit of the stabilizer G_α on S ∖ {α}, the size of G_α is at most f(d), where d is the length of that orbit.
nodes.by: Proposed by Charles Sims; proved by Peter Cameron, Cheryl Praeger, Jan Saxl and Gary Seitz
nodes.note: The proof uses the classification of finite simple groups. A consequence is that there are only finitely many connected distance-transitive graphs of degree greater than 2.

nodes.name: Krasner–Kaloujnine universal embedding theorem
nodes.statement: If a group G has a normal subgroup A and H = G/A, then there is an injective homomorphism from G into the regular wreath product A Wr H. Equivalently, every group extension of H by A is isomorphic to a subgroup of A Wr H.
nodes.by: Marc Krasner and Lev Kaluznin, 1951
nodes.note: The group A Wr H is called universal with respect to all extensions of H by A.

nodes.name: Leray's theorem
nodes.statement: Let F be a sheaf on a topological space X and U an open cover of X. If the sheaf cohomology groups Hᵏ(V, F) vanish for all k ≥ 1 on every finite intersection V of sets from U, then for every q ≥ 0 the q-th Čech cohomology group of F with respect to U is isomorphic to the q-th sheaf cohomology group of F on X.
nodes.by: Named after Jean Leray
nodes.note: It relates abstract sheaf cohomology with Čech cohomology.

nodes.name: Levi decomposition
nodes.statement: Every finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a field of characteristic zero is the semidirect product of a solvable ideal (its radical) and a semisimple subalgebra.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Wilhelm Killing and Élie Cartan; proved by Levi, 1905
nodes.note: It reduces problems about finite-dimensional Lie algebras and Lie groups to separate problems about solvable and semisimple ones. Malcev (1942) showed that any two Levi subalgebras are conjugate by an inner automorphism.

nodes.name: Levitzky's theorem
nodes.statement: In a right Noetherian ring, every nil one-sided ideal is nilpotent.
nodes.by: Jacob Levitzki, submitted 1939 (published 1950); a particularly simple proof by Utumi, 1963
nodes.note: It is one of the results suggesting that the Köthe conjecture is true, and it solved one of Köthe's questions.

nodes.name: Maschke's theorem
nodes.statement: Let G be a finite group and K a field whose characteristic does not divide the number of elements of G. Then every subrepresentation of a representation of G over K has a complementary subrepresentation, so every finite-dimensional representation of G over K is a direct sum of irreducible ones. Equivalently, the group algebra K[G] is semisimple.
nodes.by: Named after Heinrich Maschke
nodes.note: The converse also holds: if the characteristic of K divides the order of G, then K[G] is not semisimple. The theorem fails for infinite groups such as the integers.

nodes.name: Hilbert's basis theorem
nodes.statement: Every ideal of a polynomial ring in finitely many variables over a field has a finite generating set. More generally, if R is a Noetherian ring, then the polynomial ring R[X] is also Noetherian.
nodes.by: David Hilbert, 1890
nodes.note: It implies that every algebraic set is the intersection of a finite number of hypersurfaces. Hilbert's original proof is non-constructive.

nodes.name: Cayley–Hamilton theorem
nodes.statement: Every square matrix A over a commutative ring satisfies its own characteristic equation. That is, if p_A(λ) = det(λI − A), then p_A(A) = 0, the zero matrix.
nodes.by: Special case proved by William Rowan Hamilton, 1853; Cayley stated it for 3×3 and smaller matrices in 1858; the general case was first proved by Ferdinand Frobenius, 1878
nodes.note: It lets the n-th power of an n×n matrix be written as a linear combination of its lower powers. Over a field it is equivalent to saying that the minimal polynomial divides the characteristic polynomial.

nodes.name: Abel–Ruffini theorem
nodes.statement: For every degree n ≥ 5, the general polynomial equation of degree n, whose coefficients are treated as indeterminates, has no solution in radicals. A solution in radicals is a formula built from the coefficients using only addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and nth roots.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Carl Friedrich Gauss, 1798; incomplete proof by Paolo Ruffini, 1799, refined and completed 1813; proof by Niels Henrik Abel, 1824
nodes.note: The quadratic, cubic and quartic formulas solve degrees two, three and four. Galois theory shows that x⁵ − x − 1 = 0 is the simplest equation that cannot be solved in radicals.

nodes.name: Matlis duality
nodes.statement: Let R be a Noetherian complete local ring with residue field k, let E be an injective hull of k, and define the dual of a module M as Hom_R(M,E). Then this duality functor is an anti-equivalence between the categories of Artinian and Noetherian R-modules, and in particular an anti-equivalence from the category of finite-length modules to itself.
nodes.by: General case introduced by Matlis, 1958; the special case where the local ring contains a field mapping to the residue field is closely related to earlier work by Francis Sowerby Macaulay
nodes.note: It is a duality between Artinian and Noetherian modules over a complete Noetherian local ring. The special case related to Macaulay's work is sometimes called Macaulay duality.

nodes.name: Matrix determinant lemma
nodes.statement: If A is an invertible square matrix and u, v are column vectors, then det(A + uvᵀ) = (1 + vᵀA⁻¹u) det(A). In terms of the adjugate matrix, det(A + uvᵀ) = det(A) + vᵀ adj(A) u, which holds whether or not A is invertible.
nodes.note: It gives the determinant of the sum of an invertible matrix and the outer product of two vectors. Together with the Sherman–Morrison formula it lets both the inverse and the determinant be updated cheaply.

nodes.name: Matsumoto's theorem
nodes.statement: Take a Coxeter group given by generators x with relations x² = 1 and Artin relations xyxy… = yxyx… (both sides of the same length) from its presentation. If two reduced words represent the same element, the first can be turned into the second by repeatedly applying these Artin relations, so the two words are equivalent under the Artin relations alone.
nodes.by: Hideya Matsumoto, 1964
nodes.note: It is sometimes called Matsumoto's lemma. It gives a natural map, not a group homomorphism, from a Coxeter group to the corresponding braid group.

nodes.name: Euler's rotation theorem
nodes.statement: In three-dimensional space, any displacement of a rigid body that leaves one point of the body fixed is equivalent to a single rotation about some axis through that fixed point.
nodes.by: Leonhard Euler, 1775
nodes.note: It follows that the composition of two rotations is a rotation, so the rotations form a group.

nodes.name: Mumford vanishing theorem
nodes.statement: Let X be a complex projective manifold and L a semi-ample invertible sheaf on X with Iitaka dimension at least 2. Then the cohomology groups Hⁱ(X, L⁻¹) are zero for i = 0 and i = 1.
nodes.by: Mumford, 1967
nodes.note: It is related to the Ramanujam vanishing theorem and is generalized by the Kawamata–Viehweg vanishing theorem.

nodes.name: Nagao's theorem
nodes.statement: Let K be a field. The group GL₂(K[t]) of invertible 2-by-2 matrices over the polynomial ring K[t] is the amalgamated product of GL₂(K) and B(K[t]) over their intersection B(K), where B(R) is the group of upper triangular matrices with entries a, b, d, in which a and d are units of R and b is any element of R.
nodes.by: Named after Hirosi Nagao
nodes.note: Jean-Pierre Serre extended it to describe the corresponding matrix group over the coordinate ring of a projective curve.

nodes.name: Nakai conjecture
nodes.statement: If V is a complex algebraic variety whose ring of differential operators is generated by the derivations it contains, then V is a smooth variety.
nodes.by: Yoshikazu Nakai, 1961
nodes.note: The converse is a result of Alexander Grothendieck. The conjecture is known to be true for algebraic curves and Stanley–Reisner rings, and a proof would also establish the Zariski–Lipman conjecture.

nodes.name: Noether's theorem on rationality for surfaces
nodes.statement: Let S be a non-singular projective complex algebraic surface. If there is a morphism φ from S to the projective line whose general fibre is also a projective line, then S is rational.
nodes.by: Max Noether
nodes.note: It gives a criterion for a surface to be rational.

nodes.name: Norm residue isomorphism theorem
nodes.statement: For a field k, an integer ℓ that is invertible in k and every natural number n, the norm residue map (Galois symbol) from the Milnor K-group Kₙᴹ(k) modulo ℓ to the étale cohomology group Hⁿ(k, μℓ⊗ⁿ), with coefficients in the n-th tensor power of the ℓ-th roots of unity, is an isomorphism.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Spencer Bloch and Kazuya Kato (John Milnor had speculated the case ℓ = 2); proved by Vladimir Voevodsky using results of Markus Rost
nodes.note: The case ℓ = 2 is Milnor's conjecture. The result lets techniques that work on Milnor K-groups be applied to Galois cohomology and the other way round.

nodes.name: Nullity theorem
nodes.statement: Take an invertible matrix split into four blocks, and split its inverse by the transposed partition. Then the nullity (the dimension of the kernel) of each block equals the nullity of the complementary block of the inverse. More generally, the nullity of any submatrix equals the nullity of the complementary submatrix of the inverse.
nodes.by: Proven in an abstract setting by Gustafson, 1984, and for matrices by Fiedler and Markham, 1986
nodes.note: For blocks A, B, C, D of the matrix and E, F, G, H of its inverse, nullity A = nullity H, nullity B = nullity F, nullity C = nullity G and nullity D = nullity E.

nodes.name: Oka coherence theorem
nodes.statement: The sheaf of holomorphic functions on ℂⁿ is coherent. The same holds for the sheaf of holomorphic functions on any complex manifold.
nodes.by: Kiyoshi Oka, 1950

nodes.name: Pieri's formula
nodes.statement: The product of the Schur function s_μ and the complete homogeneous symmetric polynomial h_r is the sum of s_λ over all partitions λ obtained from μ by adding r elements, no two in the same column. The dual rule for the elementary symmetric polynomial e_r is the same with no two added elements in the same row.
nodes.by: Named after Mario Pieri
nodes.note: It implies Giambelli's formula. The Littlewood–Richardson rule generalizes it to the product of any two Schur functions.

nodes.name: Ping-pong lemma
nodes.statement: Let a group G act on a set X, and let H₁, …, H_k (k ≥ 2) be subgroups of G, at least one of which has more than 2 elements. If there are pairwise disjoint nonempty subsets X₁, …, X_k of X such that every element h ≠ 1 of H_i maps X_s into X_i whenever i ≠ s, then the subgroup generated by H₁, …, H_k is their free product H₁ ∗ … ∗ H_k.
nodes.by: The ping-pong argument is commonly attributed to Felix Klein, late 19th century; this version appears in Olijnyk and Suchchansky, 2004, with a proof from de la Harpe, 2000
nodes.note: It was a key tool in Jacques Tits's 1972 proof of the Tits alternative. A corollary for elements of infinite order shows that suitable elements a₁, …, a_k generate a free group with basis {a₁, …, a_k}.

nodes.name: Chevalley–Warning theorem
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field of characteristic p, and let f₁, …, f_r be polynomials in n variables over F whose total degrees d₁, …, d_r satisfy n > d₁ + … + d_r. Then the number of common solutions of f₁ = … = f_r = 0 in Fⁿ is divisible by p.
nodes.by: Warning, 1935; the slightly weaker Chevalley's theorem was proved by Chevalley, 1935
nodes.note: It implies Chevalley's theorem: if such a system has no constant terms, it has a non-trivial solution. Chevalley's theorem implied the conjecture of Artin and Dickson that finite fields are quasi-algebraically closed.

nodes.name: Principal axis theorem
nodes.statement: Every quadratic form on ℝⁿ can be written Q(x) = xᵀAx with A a symmetric matrix; the eigenvalues λ₁, …, λₙ of A are real, and A has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors u₁, …, uₙ. In the coordinates c = [u₁, …, uₙ]ᵀx one has Q(x) = λ₁c₁² + … + λₙcₙ², the i-th principal axis is the line spanned by uᵢ, and the principal axes are perpendicular.
nodes.note: It is a geometrical counterpart of the spectral theorem and generalizes completing the square. It has applications to principal components analysis and the singular value decomposition.

nodes.name: Quillen's lemma
nodes.statement: Let 𝔤 be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a field k. Then every endomorphism of a simple module over the enveloping algebra of 𝔤 is algebraic over k.
nodes.by: Quillen
nodes.note: Unlike a version of Schur's lemma due to Dixmier, it does not require k to be uncountable. Quillen's original short proof uses generic flatness.

nodes.name: Quillen–Suslin theorem
nodes.statement: Every finitely generated projective module over a polynomial ring k[x₁, …, xₙ] over a field k is free. Geometrically, every algebraic vector bundle on affine space over a field is trivial.
nodes.by: Question raised by Jean-Pierre Serre, 1955; proved independently by Daniel Quillen and Andrei Suslin, 1976
nodes.note: It was long known as Serre's conjecture. Leonid Vaseršteĭn later gave a simpler and much shorter proof.

nodes.name: Ramanujam–Samuel theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be a local Noetherian ring with maximal ideal m, whose completion is integral and integrally closed. Let ρ be a local homomorphism from A to a local Noetherian ring B of larger dimension, such that B is formally smooth over A and the residue field of B is finite over that of A. Then a cycle of codimension 1 in Spec(B) that is principal at the point mB is principal.
nodes.by: Introduced independently by Samuel, 1962, in answer to a question of Grothendieck, and by C. P. Ramanujam in an appendix to a paper by Seshadri, 1963; generalized by Grothendieck, 1967
nodes.note: It gives conditions for a divisor of a local ring to be principal. The form stated here is Grothendieck's version.

nodes.name: Regev's theorem
nodes.statement: The tensor product of two PI algebras is a PI algebra.
nodes.by: Amitai Regev

nodes.name: Reider's theorem
nodes.statement: Let D be a nef divisor on a smooth projective surface X with canonical divisor K_X. If D² > 4, then the linear system |K_X+D| has no base points unless some nonzero effective divisor E has D·E = 0 and E² = −1, or D·E = 1 and E² = 0; if D² > 8, then |K_X+D| is very ample unless some nonzero effective divisor E has D·E = 0 and E² = −1 or −2, or D·E = 1 and E² = 0 or −1, or D·E = 2 and E² = 0, or D·E = 3, D = 3E and E² = 1.
nodes.note: It gives conditions for a line bundle on a projective surface to be very ample, and it implies the surface case of the Fujita conjecture.

nodes.name: Riemann–Roch theorem for surfaces
nodes.statement: If D is a divisor on a non-singular projective surface, then χ(D) = χ(0) + ½ D·(D − K). Here χ is the holomorphic Euler characteristic, the dot is the intersection number, and K is the canonical divisor.
nodes.by: Classical form first given by Castelnuovo, after preliminary versions by Noether (1886) and Enriques (1894); the sheaf-theoretic version is due to Hirzebruch
nodes.note: The constant χ(0) equals 1 + p_a, where p_a is the arithmetic genus of the surface. For a curve, the corresponding statement is χ(D) = χ(0) + deg(D).

nodes.name: Rota's basis conjecture
nodes.statement: Let X be a vector space of dimension n, or more generally a matroid of rank n, with n disjoint bases B₁, …, Bₙ. Then the elements of these bases can be arranged in an n × n matrix whose rows are exactly the given bases and whose columns are also bases.
nodes.by: Gian-Carlo Rota, 1989; first published by Huang and Rota, 1994
nodes.note: It has been proven for paving matroids for all n and for all matroids when n ≤ 3. For vector spaces over the real numbers it is known to be true for infinitely many values of n.

nodes.name: Schlessinger's theorem
nodes.statement: Let Λ be a complete Noetherian local ring with residue field k, and C the category of local Artinian Λ-algebras with residue field k. A functor F from C to sets with F(k) a single element has a hull if it satisfies H1 to H3, and is representable by a complete Noetherian local algebra if it also satisfies H4, where: (H1) the map F(Y ×_X Z) → F(Y) ×_{F(X)} F(Z) is surjective whenever Z → X is a small extension (a surjection whose kernel is a 1-dimensional k-vector space) and Y → X is any morphism in C; (H2) this map is a bijection when Z → X is k[x]/(x²) → k; (H3) the tangent space of F is finite-dimensional over k; (H4) this map is a bijection whenever Y = Z is a small extension of X with the same map to X.
nodes.by: Schlessinger, 1968
nodes.note: It refines Grothendieck's 1960 theorem that such a functor is pro-representable if and only if it preserves all finite limits; Schlessinger's conditions only involve pullbacks of a special form, which are easier to check.

nodes.name: Schreier refinement theorem
nodes.statement: Any two subnormal series of subgroups of a given group have equivalent refinements. Two series are equivalent if there is a bijection between their factor groups that sends each factor group to an isomorphic one.
nodes.by: Otto Schreier, 1928
nodes.note: It gives an elegant proof of the Jordan–Hölder theorem and is often proved using the Zassenhaus lemma.

nodes.name: Schur–Weyl duality
nodes.statement: The symmetric group S_k (permuting the factors) and the general linear group GL_n (multiplying every factor by the same invertible matrix) act with commuting actions on the k-fold tensor product of ℂⁿ, and under their joint action this space splits as a direct sum, over Young diagrams D with k boxes and at most n rows, of products π_D ⊗ ρ_D of an irreducible representation π_D of S_k and an irreducible representation ρ_D of GL_n, where different D give non-isomorphic representations for each group. In its abstract form, the algebras of operators generated by the two actions are each other's full centralizers in the algebra of endomorphisms of the tensor space.
nodes.by: Issai Schur discovered the phenomenon; Hermann Weyl popularized it
nodes.note: It can be proven using the double centralizer theorem. For k = 2 it says that two-tensors split into symmetric and antisymmetric parts, each irreducible for GL_n.

nodes.name: Schur–Horn theorem
nodes.statement: Take two non-increasing sequences of real numbers d₁ ≥ … ≥ d_N and λ₁ ≥ … ≥ λ_N. A Hermitian matrix with eigenvalues λ₁, …, λ_N and diagonal entries d₁, …, d_N exists if and only if the two sequences have the same sum and, for every n from 1 to N, the sum of the first n of the d's is at most the sum of the first n of the λ's.
nodes.by: Named after Issai Schur and Alfred Horn; the necessity direction is Schur's theorem and the converse is Horn's theorem
nodes.note: It can be viewed as a corollary of the Atiyah–Guillemin–Sternberg convexity theorem, and it has inspired generalizations in symplectic geometry such as Kostant's convexity theorem.

nodes.name: Schwartz–Zippel lemma
nodes.statement: Let P be a non-zero polynomial in n variables of total degree d over an integral domain R, and let S be a finite subset of R. If r_1, …, r_n are chosen independently and uniformly at random from S, then the probability that P(r_1, …, r_n) = 0 is at most d / |S|.
nodes.by: Discovered independently by Jack Schwartz, Richard Zippel, and Richard DeMillo and Richard J. Lipton (DeMillo and Lipton a year earlier); the finite field version was proved by Øystein Ore, 1922
nodes.note: It is used for probabilistic polynomial identity testing: evaluating a nonzero polynomial at random points of a large enough set is likely to give a nonzero value. The bound is attained by a product of d linear factors in one variable when d ≤ |S|.

nodes.name: Shapiro's lemma
nodes.statement: Let R → S be a ring homomorphism, M a left S-module (also regarded as a left R-module by restriction of scalars) and N a left R-module. If S is projective as a right R-module, then Ext^n_R(N, M) ≅ Ext^n_S(S ⊗_R N, M) for every n ≥ 0. If S is projective as a left R-module, then Ext^n_R(M, N) ≅ Ext^n_S(M, Hom_R(S, N)) for every n ≥ 0.
nodes.by: Arnold S. Shapiro, 1961; discovered earlier by Beno Eckmann, 1953
nodes.note: It relates extensions of modules over one ring to extensions over another, in particular the cohomology of a group to the cohomology of a subgroup.

nodes.name: Short five lemma
nodes.statement: In an abelian category, or in the category of groups, let a commutative diagram have two rows that are short exact sequences 0 → A → B → C → 0 and 0 → A′ → B′ → C′ → 0, joined by maps g: A → A′, f: B → B′ and h: C → C′. If g and h are isomorphisms, then f is an isomorphism as well.
nodes.note: It is a special case of the five lemma. The middle map must exist and make the diagram commute; objects that merely have isomorphic sub- and factor objects need not be isomorphic.

nodes.name: Sinkhorn's theorem
nodes.statement: If A is an n × n matrix with strictly positive entries, then there exist diagonal matrices D₁ and D₂ with strictly positive diagonal entries such that D₁AD₂ is doubly stochastic, meaning that every row and every column sums to 1. D₁ and D₂ are unique up to multiplying the first by a positive number and dividing the second by the same number.
nodes.note: The scaled matrix can be approached by alternately rescaling all rows and all columns of A to sum to 1, the Sinkhorn–Knopp algorithm. In the 2010s the theorem came to be used to solve entropy-regularised optimal transport problems.

nodes.name: Specht's theorem
nodes.statement: Two complex square matrices A and B of the same size are unitarily equivalent (B = U*AU for some unitary matrix U) if and only if tr W(A, A*) = tr W(B, B*) for every word W in two variables. A word is a product x^m₁ y^n₁ x^m₂ y^n₂ ⋯ x^mₚ with non-negative integer exponents.
nodes.by: Wilhelm Specht, 1940
nodes.note: The theorem gives infinitely many trace conditions, but a finite subset suffices for matrices of a given size. For 2×2 matrices three conditions are enough.

nodes.name: Stallings theorem about ends of groups
nodes.statement: A finitely generated group G has more than one end (its Cayley graph has more than one connected component at infinity) if and only if G splits nontrivially as an amalgamated free product or an HNN extension over a finite subgroup. Equivalently, G acts on a simplicial tree without a global fixed point, with finite edge-stabilizers and without edge-inversions.
nodes.by: John R. Stallings, 1968 (torsion-free case) and 1971 (general case)
nodes.note: For torsion-free finitely generated groups it implies that G has infinitely many ends if and only if G is a free product of two nontrivial groups. It is considered one of the first results in geometric group theory.

nodes.name: Strassmann's theorem
nodes.statement: Let K be a field with a non-Archimedean absolute value and let R be its valuation ring. If f(x) = a₀ + a₁x + a₂x² + … is a formal power series that is not identically zero, with coefficients in R that converge to zero, then f has at most N zeros in R, where N is the largest index with |a_N| equal to the largest of the |aₙ|.
nodes.by: Introduced by Reinhold Strassman
nodes.note: It can be used to prove the Skolem–Mahler–Lech theorem on the zeros of linear recurrence sequences. The Weierstrass preparation theorem generalises it.

nodes.name: Weinstein–Aronszajn identity
nodes.statement: Let A be an m × n matrix and B an n × m matrix, either or both possibly infinite, such that AB (and hence also BA) is of trace class. Then det(I_m + AB) = det(I_n + BA), where I_k is the k × k identity matrix.
nodes.note: It is closely related to the matrix determinant lemma and is the determinant analogue of the Woodbury matrix identity for matrix inverses. It implies that AB and BA have the same non-zero eigenvalues.

nodes.name: Wedderburn–Artin theorem
nodes.statement: An Artinian semisimple ring is isomorphic to a product of finitely many matrix rings, the i-th being nᵢ-by-nᵢ matrices over a division ring Dᵢ. The integers nᵢ and the division rings Dᵢ are uniquely determined up to the order of the factors. In particular, any simple left or right Artinian ring is an n-by-n matrix ring over a division ring D, with n and D uniquely determined.
nodes.by: Joseph Wedderburn, for finite-dimensional simple algebras over a field; generalized by Emil Artin to simple left or right Artinian rings
nodes.note: It classifies semisimple rings and semisimple algebras. For a finite-dimensional semisimple algebra over a field k, each Dᵢ is a finite-dimensional division algebra over k.

nodes.name: Theorem of Bertini
nodes.statement: Let X be a smooth quasi-projective variety over an algebraically closed field, embedded in projective space ℙⁿ. Then the set of hyperplanes that do not contain X and meet X in a smooth intersection contains an open dense subset of the system of all hyperplanes. This set is itself open if X is projective, and if dim X ≥ 2 the intersections are connected, hence irreducible.
nodes.by: Eugenio Bertini
nodes.note: A general hyperplane section of X is smooth, so smoothness is a generic property. It is the simplest and broadest of the Bertini theorems, with no restriction on the characteristic of the field.

nodes.name: Theorem of the cube
nodes.statement: Let U, V and W be complete varieties over an algebraically closed field, with points u, v and w on them. Any invertible sheaf L on U×V×W whose restrictions to U×V×{w}, U×{v}×W and {u}×V×W are all trivial is itself trivial.
nodes.by: First discovered in the context of linear equivalence by the Italian school of algebraic geometry; modern version first published by Serge Lang, who credited it to André Weil; treated with sheaf cohomology by David Mumford
nodes.note: It gives a condition for a line bundle over a product of three complete varieties to be trivial. The theorem of the square for abelian varieties is a corollary, also due to Weil.

nodes.name: Hilbert's syzygy theorem
nodes.statement: If M is a finitely generated module over a polynomial ring k[x₁, …, xₙ] in n indeterminates over a field k, then the nth syzygy module of M is a free module, so M has projective dimension at most n. The theorem also holds for modules that are not finitely generated, so the global dimension of k[x₁, …, xₙ] is n.
nodes.by: David Hilbert, 1890
nodes.note: It is one of three fundamental theorems about polynomial rings over fields, with Hilbert's basis theorem and Hilbert's Nullstellensatz. It is now considered an early result of homological algebra.

nodes.name: Thompson order formula
nodes.statement: Suppose a finite group G has exactly two conjugacy classes of involutions (elements of order 2), with representatives t and z. Then |G| = |C_G(z)|·a(t) + |C_G(t)|·a(z), where C_G denotes the centralizer and a(x) is the number of pairs (u,v) with u conjugate to t, v conjugate to z, and x in the subgroup generated by uv.
nodes.by: Introduced by John Griggs Thompson (Held, 1969); it extends results of Brauer and Fowler, 1955
nodes.note: It gives the order of a finite group in terms of the centralizers of involutions. Harris gave a more complicated version for groups with more than two conjugacy classes of involutions.

nodes.name: Thompson transitivity theorem
nodes.statement: Let G be a finite group and p a prime such that all p-local subgroups of G are p-constrained. If A is a self-centralizing normal abelian subgroup of a Sylow p-subgroup of G and A has rank at least 3, then the centralizer C_G(A) acts transitively on the maximal A-invariant q-subgroups of G, for any prime q ≠ p.
nodes.by: Originated in the proof of the odd order theorem by Feit and Thompson, 1963
nodes.note: It was used to prove the Thompson uniqueness theorem.

nodes.name: Thompson uniqueness theorem
nodes.statement: In a minimal simple finite group of odd order, there is a unique maximal subgroup containing a given elementary abelian subgroup of rank 3.
nodes.by: Feit and Thompson, 1963; shorter proof by Bender, 1970

nodes.name: Three subgroups lemma
nodes.statement: Let X, Y and Z be subgroups of a group G. If the commutator subgroups [[X,Y],Z] and [[Y,Z],X] are both trivial, then [[Z,X],Y] is trivial. More generally, for a normal subgroup N of G, if [[X,Y],Z] and [[Y,Z],X] are contained in N, then [[Z,X],Y] is contained in N.
nodes.note: It is a consequence of the Hall–Witt identity of Philip Hall and Ernst Witt.

nodes.name: Torelli theorem
nodes.statement: A non-singular projective algebraic curve (compact Riemann surface) over the complex numbers is determined by its Jacobian variety, when that is given as a principally polarized abelian variety. The same holds over any algebraically closed field.
nodes.by: Named after Ruggiero Torelli
nodes.note: It can be recast as saying that the period mapping from the moduli space of curves of a fixed genus to a moduli space of abelian varieties is injective on geometric points.

nodes.name: Trichotomy theorem
nodes.statement: Every finite simple group of characteristic 2 type and rank at least 3 belongs to one of three classes: groups of GF(2) type, groups of standard type for some odd prime, or groups of uniqueness type. There are no simple groups of uniqueness type.
nodes.by: Michael Aschbacher for rank 3; Gorenstein and Lyons for rank at least 4
nodes.note: Groups of GF(2) type were classified by Timmesfeld and others. Groups of standard type were classified by the Gilman–Griess theorem and work by several others.

nodes.name: Tsen's theorem
nodes.statement: A function field K of an algebraic curve over an algebraically closed field is quasi-algebraically closed (C₁). Consequently the Brauer group of any such field vanishes, and all the Galois cohomology groups Hⁱ(K, K*) vanish for i ≥ 1.
nodes.by: Chiungtze C. Tsen, 1933
nodes.note: The result is used to calculate the étale cohomology groups of an algebraic curve.

nodes.name: Structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a principal ideal domain
nodes.statement: Every finitely generated module M over a principal ideal domain R is isomorphic to a direct sum R/(d₁) ⊕ R/(d₂) ⊕ … ⊕ R/(dₙ), where d₁, …, dₙ are non-invertible elements of R with d₁ | d₂ | … | dₙ. Some of the dᵢ may be 0, which gives free summands R, and the dᵢ (the invariant factors) are unique up to multiplication by units.
nodes.note: It generalizes the fundamental theorem of finitely generated abelian groups, which is the case R = ℤ. Applied to a linear operator on a finite-dimensional vector space, it yields the rational canonical form and the Jordan canonical form.

nodes.name: Vincent's theorem
nodes.statement: Take a polynomial with rational coefficients and no multiple roots, and apply successive substitutions x = a₁ + 1/x₁, x₁ = a₂ + 1/x₂, …, where a₁, a₂, a₃, … are any numbers greater than or equal to 1, clearing denominators each time. After enough substitutions, every transformed polynomial either has no sign variation in its coefficients, and then no positive root, or exactly one sign variation, and then exactly one positive real root.
nodes.by: Vincent, 1834 and 1836; a bisection version is due to Alesina and Galuzzi, 2000
nodes.note: It is the basis of the fastest methods for isolating the real roots of polynomials, such as the Vincent–Akritas–Strzeboński method. It was long overshadowed by Sturm's theorem.

nodes.name: Walter theorem
nodes.statement: Let G be a finite group whose Sylow 2-subgroups are abelian, and let O(G) be its largest normal subgroup of odd order. Then G/O(G) has a normal subgroup of odd index that is a product of groups, each of which is a 2-group, or a simple group PSL₂(q) with q = 2ⁿ or q ≡ 3 or 5 mod 8, or the Janko group J1, or a Ree group ²G₂(3^(2n+1)).
nodes.by: Proved by Walter; Bender (1970) gave a simpler proof using Bender's method; Thompson and Bombieri, Odlyzko and Hunt (1980) later showed the groups with Ree-like subgroup structure are Ree groups
nodes.note: The original statement only said that the corresponding groups have a subgroup structure similar to Ree groups.

nodes.name: Weyl character formula
nodes.statement: Let π be an irreducible finite-dimensional representation of a complex semisimple Lie algebra with Cartan subalgebra 𝔥, and let λ be its highest weight. Then at every H in 𝔥 where the denominator is not zero, the character ch_π(H) = tr(e^(π(H))) equals ∑_{w∈W} ε(w) e^(w(λ+ρ)(H)) divided by ∏_{α∈Δ⁺} (e^(α(H)/2) − e^(−α(H)/2)), where W is the Weyl group, Δ⁺ the set of positive roots, ρ half the sum of the positive roots, and ε(w) = (−1)^ℓ(w).
nodes.by: Hermann Weyl
nodes.note: The same formula gives the characters of irreducible representations of compact connected Lie groups on a maximal torus. The Weyl dimension formula and the Kostant multiplicity formula follow from it, and for the trivial representation it becomes the Weyl denominator formula.

nodes.name: Witt's theorem
nodes.statement: Let V be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field k of characteristic different from 2 with a non-degenerate symmetric or skew-symmetric bilinear form. Then every isometry between two subspaces of V extends to an isometry of the whole of V.
nodes.by: Named after Ernst Witt
nodes.note: It implies that all maximal totally isotropic subspaces of V have the same dimension, and it allows the definition of the Witt group W(k), which describes the stable theory of quadratic forms over k.

nodes.name: Witten conjecture
nodes.statement: Let F be the generating function whose coefficients are the intersection numbers ⟨τ_d1,…,τ_dn⟩ of the products of c₁(L_i)^d_i on the Deligne–Mumford compactification of the moduli stack of genus g Riemann surfaces with n marked points, over all g and n, where L_i is the line bundle given by the cotangent space at the i-th marked point. Then Z = exp F is a τ-function for the KdV hierarchy, that is, it satisfies a certain series of partial differential equations corresponding to the basis {L₋₁, L₀, L₁, …} of the Virasoro algebra.
nodes.by: Introduced by Edward Witten, 1991; proved by Maxim Kontsevich, 1992
nodes.note: Witten's motivation was that two different models of 2-dimensional quantum gravity should have the same partition function. The Virasoro conjecture generalizes it.

nodes.name: Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula
nodes.statement: For X and Y in the Lie algebra of a Lie group, the solution Z of e^X e^Y = e^Z can be written as a formal series built from X, Y and their iterated commutators, beginning Z = X + Y + ½[X,Y] + (1/12)[X,[X,Y]] + (1/12)[Y,[Y,X]] + …. If X and Y are sufficiently small, this series converges and its sum Z satisfies e^X e^Y = e^Z.
nodes.by: Named after Henry Frederick Baker, John Edward Campbell and Felix Hausdorff, who stated its qualitative form; foreshadowed by Friedrich Schur, 1890; noted in print by Campbell, 1897; first explicit formula with all coefficients by Eugene Dynkin, 1947
nodes.note: Near the identity, group multiplication in a Lie group can be expressed in purely Lie algebraic terms. The formula gives comparatively simple proofs of deep results in the Lie group–Lie algebra correspondence.

nodes.name: Glauberman's Z* theorem
nodes.statement: Let G be a finite group and let O(G) be its largest normal subgroup of odd order. If T is a Sylow 2-subgroup of G that contains an involution which is not conjugate in G to any other element of T, then that involution lies in Z*(G), the inverse image in G of the center of G/O(G).
nodes.by: George Glauberman, 1966
nodes.note: It generalizes the Brauer–Suzuki theorem, and its proof uses the Brauer–Suzuki theorem to deal with some small cases.

nodes.name: Glauberman's ZJ theorem
nodes.statement: Let p be an odd prime and let G be a finite group that is p-constrained and p-stable and has a nontrivial normal p-subgroup. Then for any Sylow p-subgroup S of G, the product of the largest normal subgroup of G whose order is coprime to p with Z(J(S)) is a normal subgroup of G. Here J(S) is the subgroup of S generated by its abelian subgroups of maximal order, and Z denotes the center.
nodes.by: George Glauberman

nodes.name: Zariski's lemma
nodes.statement: If a field K is finitely generated as an associative algebra over another field k, then K is a finite field extension of k, that is, K is a finite dimensional vector space over k.
nodes.by: Zariski, 1947
nodes.note: An important application is a proof of the weak form of Hilbert's Nullstellensatz. The lemma also follows from the Noether normalization lemma.

nodes.name: Zariski's main theorem
nodes.statement: A birational morphism with finite fibers to a normal variety is an isomorphism onto an open subset.
nodes.by: Zariski, 1943
nodes.note: The theorem is stated in several related ways. Another form says that the total transform of a normal point under a proper birational morphism is connected. It is the special case of Zariski's connectedness theorem for birational varieties.

nodes.name: Eakin–Nagata theorem
nodes.statement: Let A ⊂ B be commutative rings such that B is finitely generated as a module over A. If B is a Noetherian ring, then A is a Noetherian ring.
nodes.by: Paul M. Eakin (thesis, 1968) and, independently, Nagata (1968)
nodes.note: The converse is also true and is easier. The theorem is similar to the Artin–Tate lemma.

nodes.name: Kaplansky's theorem on projective modules
nodes.statement: Every projective module over a local ring is free. Here a ring, not necessarily commutative, is called local if for each element x, either x or 1 − x is a unit element.
nodes.by: First proved by Irving Kaplansky
nodes.note: For finitely generated modules over a commutative local ring it is an easy consequence of Nakayama's lemma.

nodes.name: Serre's inequality on height
nodes.statement: Let A be a Noetherian regular ring and let 𝔭 and 𝔮 be prime ideals of A. Then for every prime ideal 𝔯 that is minimal over the sum 𝔭 + 𝔮, ht(𝔯) ≤ ht(𝔭) + ht(𝔮).
nodes.by: Named after Serre, who gave a proof
nodes.note: Without the assumption that the ring is regular, the inequality can fail.

nodes.name: Binet–Cauchy identity
nodes.statement: For any real or complex numbers (or elements of a commutative ring) a_i, b_i, c_i, d_i with i = 1, …, n: (∑ a_i c_i)(∑ b_j d_j) = (∑ a_i d_i)(∑ b_j c_j) + ∑ over i<j of (a_i b_j − a_j b_i)(c_i d_j − c_j d_i).
nodes.by: Named after Jacques Philippe Marie Binet and Augustin-Louis Cauchy
nodes.note: It gives Lagrange's identity as a special case, and is itself a special case of the Cauchy–Binet formula for matrix determinants.

nodes.name: Wedderburn's little theorem
nodes.statement: Every finite division ring is a field. Consequently, every finite domain is a field.
nodes.by: Joseph Wedderburn, 1905, whose first proof had a gap; first correct proof by Leonard Eugene Dickson shortly afterwards
nodes.note: For finite rings there is no distinction between domains, division rings and fields. The Artin–Zorn theorem extends it to alternative rings.

nodes.name: Stahl's theorem
nodes.statement: Let A and B be n×n Hermitian matrices with B positive semidefinite, and define f(t) = tr(exp(A − tB)) for all real t ≥ 0. Then f is the Laplace transform of a non-negative Borel measure μ on [0, ∞): f(t) = ∫ e^(−ts) dμ(s) for all t ≥ 0, where μ depends on A and B.
nodes.by: Conjectured by Daniel Bessis, Pierre Moussa and Marcel Villani, 1975, as the BMV conjecture; proved by Herbert Stahl, 2011
nodes.note: Alexandre Eremenko gave a simplified proof in 2015. Otte Heinävaara's 2023 structure theorem for Hermitian matrices implies it as a corollary.

nodes.name: Gershgorin circle theorem
nodes.statement: Let A be a complex n×n matrix with entries a_ij, and for each row i let R_i be the sum of the absolute values of the entries in row i other than the diagonal entry. Then every eigenvalue of A lies in at least one of the closed discs with centre a_ii and radius R_i. The same holds for the discs built in the same way from the columns.
nodes.by: Semyon Aronovich Gershgorin, 1931
nodes.note: If the union of k of the discs is disjoint from the union of the other n − k discs, it contains exactly k eigenvalues counted with algebraic multiplicity. The theorem is used to judge preconditioners when solving matrix equations.
